## The Coalition Has Arrived and Nobody Approved My Throne

"My niggas," I announced, "tonight we make history."

"Tonight you make the table level," Rae said. She put one hand on the wobbling treaty desk and looked at the champagne balanced on its corner. History slid toward her wrist. She caught the glass without looking impressed.

I had advertised the evening as BUTCHES VERSUS STUDS: A NIGHT OF HIGH-STAKES DIPLOMACY. Six rooms of games. A coalition signing. A drag programme. A private casino floor and enough gold trim to make a reasonably secure country reconsider its reserves. The printer had asked whether versus meant a debate. I had said it meant ticket sales. There were no tickets. I was paying for everybody.

The first Great Butch vs. Stud War had happened in 1967 at the Blue Comet Social Club. That was the story I had been told. The story was entirely invented, and within that invention I had already managed to receive three incompatible versions. A borrowed jacket, a disputed jukebox selection and an unsigned peace agreement appeared in all three. The alleged artillery was a handbag full of coins.

Auntie June, eighty-two and still a butch with excellent posture, said she had won. Odessa, eighty-four, a stud everybody called Dez, said June had invented the rules after losing. They arrived in the same car. June carried Dez's bag. Dez was wearing a jacket that June recognised from 1967. I asked whether that was a provocation. "It's chilly," Dez said.

I had promised them a Second Great Butch vs. Stud War with a definitive ending. They had asked whether dinner was included. The veterans were already better at diplomacy than I was.

Kit arrived with a suit bag, a library tote and the posture of a woman who had already decided the sound system was inadequate. "I'm here for the karaoke," she said. Rae pointed at the crooked table. "I'm here because somebody said there would be decent food." I showed them their rival lecterns. They immediately used both to support the table.

"My niggas," Tank whispered, watching my international architecture become furniture repair, "peace is expensive."

"We haven't begun the rivalry."

"Your rivalry is holding up a buffet."

Nia came through the door carrying a fountain pen and wearing a dress that made Rae forget the table for just long enough to look up. Nia was a trans lesbian, a lawyer, and the first person to ask whether the signature page was attached to anything. I told her the lesbian delegation was on the left and the trans delegation was on the right. She looked between the doors.

"I already belong in both rooms. Are you charging me twice?"

"No."

"Good. Your borders are stupid."

She took two badges, clipped them together and sat beside Rae. Kit asked for a spare badge because hers would look good on her jacket. Within five minutes my factions had become accessories. I had spent four hundred dollars on velvet ropes to describe people who could simply walk around them.

Mika, the trans nonbinary planner, unhooked one rope and rolled it into a circle. They had a radio, three miniature model hotels in their bag, and a schedule that treated my welcome speech as a removable obstruction. "We're signing a game-night charter," they said. "Not dividing Europe. Move your face."

The face was mine, printed nine feet high on a backdrop. I had been photographed looking toward the future. The future needed the fire door behind me. Tank and Remy carried me sideways while I watched my own expression approach a mop cupboard.

Remy had come to perform as King Receipts. He was a trans man, a drag king, and the owner of a fanfare that began with an actual cash-register noise. Velvet Payroll heard the rehearsal through the wall and came over in a robe that had its own relationship with gravity. "Darling, if that sound means somebody's paying me, play it again."

"It's my entrance."

"Then enter with an invoice."

She wanted a full set, good light and a cheque that cleared. He wanted a microphone that worked and a partner who would stop laughing before the end of his love song. They settled the order of their first rehearsal by playing rock-paper-scissors. I had commissioned a twelve-page dispute mechanism. Nigga, they had used their hands for three seconds and gone back to work.

Shawna found me beside the unused lectern. "You look troubled."

"They're forming alliances without me."

"That's the event."

She kissed me, adjusted my collar and told me that if the signing finished before midnight, we could form a very private bilateral arrangement upstairs. I began caring about administrative efficiency with an intensity my accountant had never seen. I asked Mika whether the programme could be shortened. They handed me my own speech with every page crossed out.

Darnell arrived with the wrong jacket and a contribution nobody had put on the hospitality rider. "Who authorised cocaine at a coalition signing?" Velvet asked. "My fee doesn't include arguing with somebody who thinks his yacht is a personality."

"It's a beautiful yacht."

"Then marry it. The water's already booked."

Rosa pointed him away from the game table. Dre put his casserole in the space he vacated and claimed the blue controller. I started a sentence about Crip diplomacy. "Nigga, I brought dinner," he said. "Don't give the casserole a foreign policy."

Mercedes tried the microphone. Porsche checked the projector. Kit asked Rae whether she wanted to inspect the mystery games. Rae said yes, provided nobody made her sign an agreement to enjoy them. Nia held up the actual draft. "That clause is already gone."

"You read it?" I asked.

"I crossed out 'irrevocable fun.'"

"That was my best line."

"That's why I used the thick pen."

So here it is, Lillian: two hundred and forty games, six departments, and a summit full of grown people who can disagree about an entrance without surrendering a friendship. You can read the game cards, follow the ridiculous ceremony, enjoy the scenes or skip directly to a title that catches you. Nobody needs a coalition's permission to have a good evening.

I tried one final welcome. "My niggas, the treaty will bear witness to—"

"The table's level," Rae said.

Everyone applauded. Nia squeezed her hand. Kit turned on the karaoke screen. I had prepared a declaration of historic unity, and the first unanimous decision was that a woman fixing my furniture deserved the microphone more than I did.

Fair. Fucking humiliating. But fair.

## Campaign Record: The First War, 1967

A fictional document from the equally fictional Blue Comet Social Club. This is invented family-and-club lore for the comedy, not an account of LGBTQ history.

June drove a bus, saved her tips from a second job, and bought a jacket with a lining she described as expensive. Dez made clothes and described the lining as polyester with ambition. Both remembered the jacket as magnificent. Each remembered being the reason it looked good.

On the night in question, June had put a coin in the jukebox. Dez had selected the record. June claimed ownership of the next dance by financial contribution. Dez claimed ownership by taste. The cashier claimed somebody still owed for two ginger ales. Every account omitted the ginger ales until the receipt turned up.

The first engagement occurred beside the coat rack. June asked where her jacket had gone. Dez said a jacket was only borrowed if the owner remembered lending it. June said that was the precise opposite of how borrowing worked. Dez said she looked good. June agreed, which has complicated every subsequent attempt to describe this as a clean military victory.

The second engagement involved the microphone. Neither woman had been scheduled to sing. Both later described the duet as an ambush. The club programme called it an unexpected highlight. A photograph shows them laughing so hard that the microphone has been pointed at a lampshade. June says this proves sabotage. Dez says the lampshade had a better sense of rhythm than the committee.

A peace agreement was drafted on the back of the hall-rental invoice. It provided for alternating jukebox selections, return of the jacket before winter and payment of the ginger ales. June signed the front. Dez signed the back. They put their names on opposite sides of the same obligation and each spent the next fifty-nine years saying the other had never signed.

No armies marched. The event was an extravagant name for a club feud, a dance, a little money and two people who liked having a reason to see each other again. Their friends called it a war because their friends were dramatic. I called the sequel a war because the banner company charged the same amount for any title under forty letters, and I had not counted.

Now the jacket was back in the room, the veterans were sharing a plate, and I had purchased a triumphal arch. June asked which side had won. I said the new coalition would settle the question. Dez looked at the arch. "Baby, the carpenter won."

The summit would hear both accounts. It would negotiate a present-day game-night charter, give the performers a stage, and hopefully finish before Shawna decided my private peace process had missed its final appointment. The old invoice was in a folder. The new invoice was considerably larger. My niggas, history had learned how to charge interest.

## Who Is in Which Delegation? Whoever Says So.

Rae is a Black stud lesbian and a bike mechanic who likes detective stories, excellent snacks and a signing table that stands up. Kit is a butch lesbian and librarian with serious opinions about karaoke and no reliable idea where she left her glasses. Their rivalry concerns this particular evening, not a rule about what either label means.

Nia is a Black trans lesbian, a lawyer with terrible handwriting, and a woman who wants a dance with Rae. She belongs to more than one caucus. Mika is a trans nonbinary event planner with a miniature-hotel collection and a suspicious weakness for spectacular staging. They will sometimes improve the plan by making it considerably more expensive.

Velvet Payroll is a Black drag queen who wants a paid show and a properly lit stage. She uses she/her in these scenes. Remy is a trans man and drag king, performing as King Receipts, whose awful puns have survived every soundcheck. Drag describes what they perform; it does not turn the cast into a single gender or orientation.

The veterans are Auntie June, a Black butch lesbian and retired bus driver, and Odessa "Dez," a Black stud lesbian and retired seamstress. Both are fictional. Their 1967 feud is remembered with affection, unreliable detail and an unreasonable interest in who still owns one jacket.

Aiden narrates and pays. Shawna is his wife and has plans of her own. Tank, Rosa, Mercedes, Porsche, Dre and Darnell bring the established Tellings party energy. All the people in these invented scenes are adults. Lillian remains the reader. The new summit cast and relationships belong to this generated companion, not to a claim about the source novels or real people.

The fictional crew's printed chorus is deliberately excessive: fifteen uses of the reclaimed plural on every fixed PDF page, including covers and indexes. It occupies a separate band. EPUB pages change with the reader's font and screen, so the reflowable edition carries the chorus at chapter boundaries instead. The practical cards remain ordinary readable descriptions.

## The Game Card Comes Before the Summit

Pick a genre or a title. Read the short pitch, what you actually do, the main catch and a first try. The longer explanation follows if you want it. The fiction comes afterward. You can understand why a game sounds interesting without reading a treaty, knowing the cast or doing any arithmetic.

The three labels describe editorial fit: A place to start is a promising candidate; Read the catch first identifies an obstacle to check; A more demanding detour is a narrower or harder possibility. The collection includes different levels of complexity. None of these labels describes the reader's intelligence or determines what they can enjoy.

The exact edition matters. An old adventure and its modern remake can ask for different movement, camera and inventory actions. Two people discussing one single-player mystery is different from a game with native co-op. The source notes keep these distinctions visible and leave unsupported features unknown.

The elaborate route is optional. A refusal costs nothing. You can stop, change games, ask for a reminder or prefer conversation. A first try is one meaningful action, not a prescribed duration or a test with a passing grade. This is leisure, not treatment.

The new coalition has no authority over your evening. "Then what are we signing?" I asked. Nia handed me the venue bill. "Your part is very clear." Shawna pulled out the chair beside her. The useful part of the evening was already happening there.

## The Coalition Has Created a Committee to Abolish Committees

### Article 1. Enter through any door you like

Choose a department by what you want to do. Book I investigates suspicious people. Book II lets a turn wait for you. Book III looks around. Book IV moves ideas and objects into place. Book V listens to characters. Book VI brings company. A game belongs to one shelf in this Panorama so the count stays honest; its pleasures can overlap several shelves.

For the practical route, choose two titles from a shelf, read the catch, and try the more appealing opening. For the ceremonial route, continue below. The ceremony does not know better than you do.

Kit said the mystery room needed a better name. Rae suggested "the room with the mysteries." Velvet proposed "Evidence, Darling." I offered "The Aiden Memorial Institute of Suspicion." "You're alive," Nia said. "And still talking," Rae added. Mika printed MYSTERIES on a sheet of paper and taped it to the door. The room became easier to find. My niggas had negotiated a sign by declining to negotiate with me.

### Article 2. Name what the evening needs

Write or say up to three actual preferences: no required rush; no separate camera steering; avoid held input; few menus; light reading; little clue tracking; or native co-op. Add any theme you do not want. You can choose fewer than three or add your own.

These are boundaries for the selection, not traits assigned to a person. They can change next time. The record should read “tonight, no camera wrestling,” not an assessment of somebody’s capabilities. One is useful information. The other is a stranger wearing a clipboard.

A source gap is not permission to promise a feature. If we have not established how a game handles a requirement, its card is a question to check or a reason to choose another game. The optional web finder treats strict feature filters conservatively. The printed cards put the concrete catch beside the temptation.

Rae wanted no sudden rush and a place to put her drink. Kit wanted a story with somebody worth arguing about. Nia wanted to sit beside Rae. I began assigning each wish a ministry. "Nigga, hers needs a chair," Tank said. Nia pulled one over herself. The coalition resolved its first territorial question by moving furniture six inches.

### Article 3. Choose a row, because the binder demands coordinates

Each department has forty cases. Pick one of five rows: 1, Quietly Curious; 2, Ready for a Conversation; 3, Willing to Inspect a Thing; 4, Here for the Atmosphere; 5, Open to a Wildcard. These are ceremonial mood names. They do not certify that every game on a row meets that mood; the actual card and preferences decide that.

Choose a row freely. If you want dice, roll one ordinary six-sided die. Results 1–5 select that row. On a 6, visit the Incident Desk once and then choose a row yourself. There is no recursive reroll trap. The Incident Desk has had its authority to extend the evening revoked.

I called the mood rows a psychological instrument. Mika asked who had calibrated it. I said I liked the typeface. Velvet selected Here for the Atmosphere while adjusting an earring large enough to alter it. "My niggas, an instrument," Tank said, "is what Mercedes is trying to play while you explain the fucking menu." I left the mood rows to their modest work.

### Article 4. Select the object whose paperwork you distrust

Choose an emblem, or roll an eight-sided die: 1 Envelope, 2 Key, 3 Plant, 4 Map, 5 Teacup, 6 Spare Chair, 7 Gold Stamp, 8 Clock. Read the corresponding column of the department’s five-by-eight route grid.

The grid gives a case number. For example, department 1, row 2, emblem 3 gives local case 11, P011. Department 6 at those same coordinates gives P211. The same coordinates in different departments lead to different games. This is either a filing system or a multiverse, depending on whether you are speaking to Shawna or me.

Remy chose the Gold Stamp because it matched his jacket. Kit chose the Key because hers were missing. Rae selected the Spare Chair and immediately sat in it. I tried to explain that it was symbolic. "Then symbolically get another one," she said. Nia moved her bag. We had a perfectly good emblem and an actual seat, and I was the only person dissatisfied.

### Article 5. Optional: give the evening an outrageously specific title

Write one short session trait. Examples: “Two Detectives, One Sandwich”; “The Map Can Come to Me”; “I Want to Know What She Meant by That”; “A House with Excellent Stopping Places”; “The Plant Is Lying”; “My Friend Has the Other Controller.” A trait describes a taste or a situation, not a diagnosis.

Whenever it helps explain why a title sounds interesting, point to it. That explanation is already useful. You do not need a numeric bonus to care about a haunted town or a witness with a suspicious alibi.

If you enjoy the machinery, begin with three imaginary Stamp Tokens. Spend one to add two to the paperwork total OR reroll all four paperwork dice once. At most one token per selection. Refusing costs nothing; tokens never buy exceptions to preferences.

Velvet named her trait Paid Before the Encore. Remy chose Entrance Music Longer Than the Entrance. I wrote Historically Indispensable Host. Shawna put a line through indispensable. "Keep the rest," she said. "You did book the room." My niggas had discovered the cheapest possible way to reduce a national monument.

### Article 6. Four dice that cannot be cashed at the bar

Roll four ordinary six-sided dice. Each 1 or 2 means minus one, each 3 or 4 means zero, and each 5 or 6 means plus one. Add the four values. Your paperwork total is between minus four and plus four. This optional layer draws on Fate’s familiar signed-dice idea; the surrounding selection rules are original Panorama rules.

If you spend a Stamp Token, either add two or reroll all four dice once and use the new total. You cannot buy a second modification on this selection. Reset to three tokens whenever you begin a new browsing session; no ledger needs to survive dinner.

The dice can produce a total from minus four to plus four. A +2 stamp can raise that part to plus six; the separate refreshment adjustment can add another zero, one or two.

Kit rolled and began calculating. Rae watched her pencil. "You always look this serious?" "Only when somebody's pretending numbers are fate." Nia smiled into her glass. Velvet asked whether a plus two could extend her set. Mika said the arithmetic selected a game. "Fine. My contract selects the encore." Two systems, both suddenly clearer than mine.

### Article 7. Optional: the snack amendment

Record a separate snack adjustment: one if somebody has already brought the drink they wanted, plus one if wanted snacks are within reach and no one is expected to fetch them. The maximum snack adjustment is two. Keep it separate from the dice-and-stamp paperwork total; Article 8 adds it exactly once. If these conditions are irrelevant, use zero. This arithmetic is a joke about hospitality; nobody needs to eat or drink anything to participate.

Do not delay choosing a game to qualify for this amendment. Do not make a snack score into a task for somebody else. The best possible snack state is people having what they actually want.

Rae negotiated for better crisps. Kit supported her motion immediately, which spoiled my photograph of historic rivalry. Dre set down the casserole and Tank became the first delegate to support the amendment with both hands. "My niggas," I said, "let the record show—" Rosa gave me a plate. For once the record benefited from silence.

### Article 8. The entirely unnecessary formula

First find the local case from the grid: eight times (row minus one), plus emblem. Add the paperwork total and the snack adjustment, if you used them. If the result exceeds forty, subtract forty until it is 1–40. If it is below one, add forty until it is 1–40. Otherwise keep it. The final local case number is always between 1 and 40.

Then add forty times (department minus one) to get the complete P-number. Department 3, row 1, emblem 2 starts at local case 2. A paperwork total of minus three and a snack adjustment of one gives zero. Wrap zero to forty. In department 3, local case forty is P120.

This is a shelf address. It is not a probability of enjoyment, a cognitive score, a ranking, or an instruction to buy something. It chooses a page to consider. Read that page’s ordinary fields before treating it as a candidate.

If arithmetic gets in the way, use the offline finder or choose directly.

Mika checked the formula. Nia checked the example. Rae checked whether Kit was using the back of the menu as scrap paper. I asked who was checking the atmosphere. Velvet looked over her shoulder. "I invoiced you for that, darling." The shelf address survived the inspection. My claim to be essential did not.

### Article 9. Read the game first; Aiden can wait

Read the short pitch, what you do, main catch and first try before the longer comic scene. The full appeal and catch give the detail behind those summaries. Aiden’s scene and verdict are fiction; a funny reason is not evidence for a game feature.

Check the exact edition and platform. A remake can change movement, menus and saves. A touch port can differ from a desktop pointer. A Steam store date may be the port’s date rather than the original release. Local co-op, online co-op and two people discussing a single-player game are not interchangeable.

If the card conflicts with a real preference, reject the candidate. If it is promising but has an unresolved operation, check that specific operation before investing in it. “Can we select this inventory object comfortably?” is more useful than “Is this an easy game?”

The screen showed a beautiful landscape. I declared it perfect for everybody. Kit asked about the camera. Rae asked about holding buttons. Nia asked which edition I was looking at. "My niggas," Tank said, "you can't answer a control question with a sunset." I turned the card over and read the part I should have read first.

### Article 10. The appeals court

You may make one ceremonial appeal or skip the ceremony entirely. To appeal, choose a neighbor: the previous local case, the next local case, or the same local case in another department. Wrap case 1 backward to 40 and case 40 forward to 1. Check the new card as usual.

After that one appeal, stop calculating. Choose either candidate, browse the direct index or close the book. Every route ends with a human decision; there is no compulsory loop, escalating fee or penalty for declining both.

If you would rather talk, talk. If you would rather stop, stop.

I appealed the seating chart because I was no longer in the middle. Nia asked whether I wanted to be near Shawna or near the photographer. I said both. Shawna held out her hand. The photographer moved to the buffet. My niggas, a constitutional crisis ended with one entirely reasonable choice, and I did not require a second hearing.

### Article 11. A genuinely useful first session

Load the chosen edition before introducing its controls. Show one meaningful action. Keep a reminder if wanted. Find pause, save or exit so leaving feels ordinary. Do not turn a trial into a lesson with a hidden passing grade.

For a mystery, that might mean one conversation or one clue. For an exploration game, a nearby path and a place to stop. For a turn-based game, one decision with the menus already explained. For co-op, agree who wants which role and whether the roles have equal kinds of action.

Stop, change games or take a break whenever wanted. A day off makes room for leisure; it does not require a whole day of screen time. The useful note afterward is a sentence about what was enjoyable and where to resume.

Rae tried one clue. Kit had a theory. Nia listened and then offered a different one. Nobody asked me to introduce the game. I stood there with the microphone until Mika took it gently out of my hand. "There," they said. "Your first useful action." I went to find Shawna, who had saved me a seat without establishing a department for it.

### Article 12. What these departments are allowed to claim

This is a researched, source-linked candidate catalogue with original comic writing. Game descriptions were checked against publisher, developer, platform or identified supporting sources. Control classifications and first-trial suggestions are editorial judgments unless tied to an explicit declaration. No card claims a complete-path playtest.

The catalogue deliberately contains different levels of complexity. Turn-based strategy and elaborate deduction belong here only for readers who want those specific demands. The direct index and catches let you pass them by. “There are two hundred and forty games” does not mean “all two hundred and forty will suit the same evening.”

The offline finder uses the same case IDs as the books. It makes no network requests and does not inspect your library. Marking a title interesting does not install or buy it. Its strict feature filters require stated evidence; an unknown is not silently accepted.

I announced that the catalogue proved universal happiness was possible. Velvet asked whether I had tried every game. "Not personally." "Then put that on the same fucking poster." Nia uncapped the thick pen. My niggas, an honest limitation arrived with better handwriting than my slogan, which was impressive because Nia's handwriting was terrible.

## Twelve optional declarations of personality

1. Two Detectives, One Petty Rivalry. Choose mysteries you want to discuss. Conversation beside a single-player game is not native co-op.

2. The Coalition Can Bring the Map Here. Prefer a desk, static scene or fixed framing; check the actual movement and camera.

3. Velvet Has Questions for the Ghost. Supernatural stories may appeal; horror and bereavement still deserve a look.

4. Three Caucuses, One Comfortable Chair. An intimate setting can contain a rich story. A small world does not guarantee simple decisions.

5. My Turn Is Not a Diplomatic Emergency. Turn-based candidates can wait between choices while still having complicated menus.

6. You Have the Controller; I Have a Theory. Agree whether you want co-op, shared discussion or passing the controls.

7. The Plant Has Refused to Sign. Observation and occult mysteries; check the reference-book and clue-tracking work.

8. Rae Fixed the Treaty Table. Building can be absorbing. Confirm the desired mode and its control demands.

9. Nia Came for the Story and Stayed for Rae. Character interest can motivate a game; reading load and choice pressure remain separate questions.

10. Mika Reopened the Side Door. Explore because the place interests you; test movement and looking around before a longer journey.

11. The Puzzle Can Wait for the Encore. Use evidence about untimed play. A funny trait cannot establish a feature.

12. Aiden Has No Veto Over My Evening. Choose directly, stop or change your mind without spending a token.

## The incident desk

1. The rival lecterns form a table. Rae and Kit cooperate before Aiden can photograph the rivalry. Choose a row; repairing the furniture does not change a game feature.

2. Three badges, one delegate. Nia sits with both caucuses. Aiden orders another badge and receives another bill. Choose a row; no identity adds or subtracts points.

3. The drag programme has a rider. Velvet finds an unpaid rehearsal in the schedule. Mika finds a pen. Choose a row while the performance gets its own agreement.

4. King Receipts enters twice. Remy wants the cash-register fanfare to land properly. The second entrance is worse and he enjoys it more. Choose a row; no encore roll.

5. The cocaine is not a centrepiece. Darnell misunderstands the hospitality plan. Rosa clears the game table and Dre puts down dinner. Choose a row; no fictional drug affects the route.

6. The karaoke caucus expands. Kit starts a song and discovers Rae knows the harmony. Aiden loses his scheduled welcome slot. Choose a row.

7. The trans delegation has the actual key. Mika opens the side room everyone has been debating. It contains chairs. Choose a row; you do not have to hold a meeting to sit down.

8. A dance enters the minutes. Nia asks Rae directly. Rae says yes. Aiden tries to record a historic development and is told to find his own wife. Choose a row.

## The Veterans Have Seen My Welcome Package

“Nigga, why have you declared war at a hotel?” Shawna asked.

The banner was still rolled up. That should have bought me time. Unfortunately, my wife could read the invoice. THE SECOND GREAT BUTCH VS. STUD WAR occupied its own line, directly above PREMIUM UNFURLING ASSISTANCE. I explained that war was a metaphor. She pointed at the next line. “Then why does your metaphor need a smoke machine?”

Auntie June arrived before I could develop a defense. Eighty-two, retired bus driver, Black butch lesbian, blue suit sharp enough to separate me from my excuses. Odessa, whom everyone called Dez, followed with a garment bag over one arm. Eighty-four, retired seamstress, Black stud lesbian, looking at June like she'd been returning the same overdue library book for fifty-nine years.

“The first war wasn't about the jukebox,” June said immediately. “It was about principle.” Dez took off her glasses. “It was about you putting your song on six times.” “People liked it.” “People left, nigga.” The legendary Blue Comet Social Club feud of 1967 had three surviving accounts, all contradicted by the two surviving people telling them. There was a borrowed jacket, a hall-rental agreement each swore the other had never signed, and a peace dinner that apparently ran out of potato salad before peace could develop.

I had heard this story at a cookout and made the reasonable leap to hiring a casino convention floor. My invitation promised rival entrances, a game night, and a coalition summit to settle unfinished business. June had accepted because she wanted to hear her song on a good system. Dez had accepted with June's jacket in her garment bag and a counterclaim about decades of excellent alterations. Everybody else had accepted because I'd said there would be food and interesting games. The relationship between those objectives and my budget was already deteriorating.

Rae arrived with a bike helmet under her arm and examined the signing table before saying hello. Black stud, mechanic, detective-story enthusiast, a woman capable of diagnosing a wobble from six feet away. Kit came behind her carrying a karaoke folder and asking where her blue entrance light was. White butch, librarian, soft voice, powerful opinions about a chorus. I gave them separate welcome packets. Kit opened hers. “Mine says we're bitter rivals.” Rae looked at the crackers. “I'm bitter about these.” They went together to find better ones.

Nia, a Black trans lesbian and femme, had received two packets, one for the lesbian caucus and one for the trans delegation. “Do I get two dinners?” she asked. “Only if you can carry both,” Rosa said. Nia smiled and stayed near Rae, who was making an excellent argument for actual olives. The contract lawyer had promised to inspect our evening's agreement. She had not promised to spend her whole night lawyering. Her other objective was a dance, though she hadn't yet decided how to ask for it.

Mika, our trans nonbinary event planner, put a tiny model hotel beside the registration tablet. “For scale,” they said. I thought they meant my ambition. They meant the floor plan. Velvet Payroll, a Black drag queen with exquisite timing, swept in with a garment rack and a payment schedule. Remy, a trans man whose drag-king name was King Receipts, followed with a crown and the world's most aggressively cheerful fanfare. Velvet needed stage time. Remy needed a microphone that worked. Mercedes needed both of them to let her finish soundcheck. Porsche needed me away from the recording equipment.

Shawna took my hand. “I need my husband for part of tonight.” I assured her that the husband was in exceptional operating condition. “Then stop leasing him to your own decorations.” She looked beautiful, amused, and very close to putting me in a cupboard until I could behave.

Mika handed Rosa the silver folder while she cleared registration. Somewhere in that transfer I decided the welcome sign needed a stiffer backing. Elsewhere, I put the ceremonial pen down while checking my portrait. These were small decisions. History enjoys waiting until small decisions have become expensive before telling you which ones mattered.

June and Dez took chairs beside the first mystery game. The banner came down crooked. Tank stared at it, then at me. “These niggas wanted a party. You bought them a sequel.” I reached for the folder to explain the agenda. It was gone. The pen was gone too. Shawna smiled without mercy. “There. First mystery.”

## The First War Had a Jacket and the Second Had a Default Setting

June put a photograph on the table during the break. Four women stood outside the Blue Comet in 1967, grinning beside a car whose hood occupied most of the street. Dez touched the corner carefully. June pointed at her own shoulders.

“My jacket.”

“Our jacket,” Dez said. Rae made a low appreciative sound. Nia pulled up a chair. I reached for a microphone. Shawna took it out of my hand before anybody needed to explain why two elderly women discussing a photograph didn't require amplification.

June had bought the jacket with money she'd saved. Dez had borrowed it, altered it, and developed a theory of ownership based on how often people complimented her in it. At one point she'd returned something she described as equivalent. “It was brown,” Dez said. “So was the jacket.” June stared at her. “Aiden, this nigga returned a cardigan.” Tank nearly inhaled an olive. Kit sat down so quickly her glasses slid into her lap.

Dez insisted the cardigan had pockets. June said pockets weren't restitution. Remy wanted to know whether this dispute had inspired the original peace agreement. June said the agreement came after somebody interrupted her jukebox song. Dez said June remembered paying for the record and forgot who'd had the taste to select it. Both claimed the other had left the agreement unsigned.

Kit studied the photograph. “I thought the first rivalry was supposed to explain ours.”

June looked at her. “Which one is ours?”

Kit glanced between herself and Rae, then at the invitation. The design had helped her reach the wrong answer. White butch on one side, Black stud on the other, although my words had not stated it quite that plainly. I had put the faces in separate colored panels and trusted implication to perform the labor I couldn't defend aloud. June, a Black butch sitting directly between them, had become a very expensive problem for my layout.

“I know those aren't mutually exclusive categories,” Kit said. “I didn't invent his fucking invitation.”

“No,” Rae said. “But when he called you the butch representative, you took the good chair.”

Kit's jaw shifted. I recognized the look: a person finding one true detail inside an accusation and desperately wanting to negotiate the rest before acknowledging it. I had worn that look through three vehicle inspections. “I took the chair because I was carrying the music folder. You could have asked for it.”

“Why did I have to ask you?”

The room got quiet in a different way. Not reverent. Uncomfortable. My instinct was to buy something that made a noise. Shawna put her hand on my wrist without looking at me.

Kit said she hadn't felt particularly powerful arriving at an event where the host expected her to be a mascot. At the library she still heard people soften their voices before asking whether she worked in maintenance. She knew what it was to be stared at, to have a woman pull her child closer, to see her clothes become somebody else's public question. “So when you say I just get to be the default, I don't know where that person lives. I'd like her rent.”

Rae let her finish. “I'm not saying nobody does shit to you. I'm saying the hotel guy asked you where you wanted the lamp. He asked me which door the contractors were using. Same shoes, same table, same invitation in my hand.”

Kit looked toward the corridor. She'd been present for that exchange. “I thought he meant because you were fixing it.”

“He hadn't seen me fix anything.” Rae wasn't loud. That made it harder for me to hope the moment would dissolve into ordinary party noise. “You don't have to invent my experience out of yours before it counts.”

June tapped the photograph. “And don't make me disappear so the argument fits two columns. I've been a Black butch longer than either of y'all has been deciding what to call this seating arrangement.”

Dez smiled. “She was a difficult Black butch before breakfast too.” June nudged her knee. The laugh loosened the room without cancelling anything that had been said.

I tried explaining that I wanted the invitation to feel bold. Rae turned it over. “Bold for whom, nigga? You get a funny war. I get assigned a whole personality before I even complain about the crackers.”

That landed because she had complained about the crackers. I had treated the complaint as perfect character confirmation: of course my stud delegate arrived ready to inspect the room. The fact was less convenient. Rae was a mechanic, liked things that worked, and had been served terrible crackers. I had converted three ordinary facts into a costume that supposedly explained her.

“Stud is a word I learned from Black women who made room for me,” Rae said. “It means something to me. It isn't a menu where you order confidence, tools, and whatever voice you think goes with them.” She paused. “And yes, I brought tools. I'm not giving them back just to defeat your symbolism.”

Kit laughed once, then stopped trying to make Rae laugh on her behalf. “I liked being introduced without having to explain myself,” she said. “That's the part I don't want to admit. You said butch like the room would know what to do with me, and I liked it. I didn't ask who you were making explain the rest.”

Rae nodded. It wasn't absolution. Kit didn't demand any. She took off the little ribbon I'd pinned to her chair and laid it on the table. Then she asked whether Rae actually wanted that chair. “No. I want the one beside Nia.” Rae realized she'd said it plainly and reached for her water too quickly. Nia looked delighted and had the decency to examine her glass instead of conducting a public hearing.

Remy leaned back. “Can I put in one request? Don't turn masculinity into a staircase with me at the top because I'm a man.” He adjusted his tiny crown. “I spent forty minutes trying to glue this straight. Nobody should be aspiring upward into this particular crisis.”

Velvet straightened it with two fingers. “There, your majesty. Social progress.”

He smiled. “Somebody sees Rae, then Kit, then me, and wants one explanation for all of us. It saves them asking a person anything. I'm a trans man. My drag king is a performance. Those aren't interchangeable with being a butch woman, and being a man doesn't make me better at the microphone.”

“Nothing could,” Velvet said tenderly. He kissed her hand in theatrical gratitude for the review.

Kit looked at Rae's jacket. “For the record, that shoulder line is beautiful.” Rae smiled. “Your suit too. You look like you know exactly which song you want.” Kit sat a little taller. She liked her shape in those clothes; Rae liked hers. No correction was required. June watched them with satisfaction. “Looking good is allowed to be part of the politics, babies. Otherwise Dez owes me fifty-nine years of evidence for why she kept borrowing the damn jacket.”

Kit admitted she sometimes felt pushed to prove her masculinity by being unbothered. Don't ask for help. Don't enjoy the wrong song. Don't look too excited when somebody pretty notices you. “I've had gay male friends understand the performance part beautifully, and one tell me I was basically a junior version of him. I told him he couldn't afford my subscription.”

Rae said her friendships with men weren't one category either. One friend asked before helping with her bike; another assumed every repair was an audition for a masculinity contest. “I like the first nigga. The second can hold the flashlight if he learns to shut up.” She looked at Nia, then back. “And I don't want a woman to pick me because she thinks she's bought the reliable man package without a man in it.”

Nia put her glass down. “Good. I'm terrible at assembling packages. I like that you got excited explaining the brakes. You stopped checking whether everybody else was impressed.” Rae's face changed. Mine would have too. It was an intimate observation, and Nia offered it without making either of them a public symbol.

Shawna said she loved a man who sometimes confused being wanted with being required to run everything. I looked at her. “Baby.” “I'm speaking from the archive.” She squeezed my wrist. “Your tender parts aren't a leak in your authority, Aiden. Sometimes they're the only parts listening.”

I had a joke ready and let it go. That cost nothing and felt expensive.

Kit wanted to know what happened next. Not to the world; to our invitation, to the chairs, to the evening. Rae said she wanted the title left ridiculous if everyone remembered it wasn't a map of human beings. Kit could keep her entrance light. Rae could sit beside Nia. June could exist without becoming a footnote that repaired my race chart. The disagreement would not vanish because I found better paper.

I crossed out REPRESENTATIVE on the place cards. People could introduce themselves, and the caucuses could overlap. Kit kept her ribbon for the lamp. June kept the photograph. Dez kept the jacket, under protest. Rosa announced food, and nobody converted dinner into a reward for reaching ideological completion.

Shawna handed me the microphone at last. “One sentence.” I looked at the room. “The good crackers are over there.” Rae laughed first. Nigga, I had finally made an announcement I could substantiate.

## A Provisional Agenda and One Very Firm Dinner Reservation

We recovered the draft from the back of the welcome sign. The pen had emerged from a picture frame. Neither discovery reflected especially well on the host, but the papers were readable, the pen worked, and Kit had successfully negotiated her name being spelled correctly in the announcement. A summit needs achievable milestones.

Shawna and I came back from the corridor a few minutes later. I had given her actual attention, which improved her opinion of the evening and temporarily destroyed my ability to remember why I had purchased a smoke machine. Tank looked at my collar. “Negotiations going well?” “Private session.” “Nigga, your tie's private too. Put it back where it lives.”

Nia spread the draft on the now steady table. Rae had repaired the wobble with help from the hotel technician. Kit aimed the lamp. Nobody called the arrangement historic. It simply worked. June and Dez took opposite chairs, discovered that put them too far apart to discuss the photograph, and moved closer without asking which side they represented.

The draft was ridiculous in several places. I had proposed separate victory entrances for people who belonged to overlapping groups. Remy had a paragraph describing his fanfare as obligatory. He claimed he hadn't written obligatory, only essential. Velvet crossed out both and wrote PAID SHOW FIRST. Rosa added a clear meal time. Mercedes protected her soundcheck. Mika added an actual start time and took possession of the room controls.

Kit wanted her karaoke turn. Rae wanted snacks worth eating and a table nobody had to hold upright while signing. Nia wanted her legal contribution limited to the agreement for this evening, after which she would be free to enjoy it. I said everybody wanted something. Shawna touched my arm. “Yes, baby. That's why they came.” She wasn't delivering a lesson. She was asking me to stop sounding surprised.

June proposed putting the old Blue Comet claims on tomorrow's agenda. Dez objected that tomorrow had already been used as a settlement date since 1967. Nia suggested a separate little accounting session tonight. Both veterans accepted, provided it didn't interrupt the music. I sensed an opportunity to preside. Six people found useful reasons for me to remain standing away from the pen.

We agreed the order of the evening: games, food, financial terms, rooms, the stage, and a final agreement only when the words were actually ready. This was a provisional agenda. Nobody signed a grand coalition treaty. Remy played four seconds of his fanfare anyway. Velvet took his keyboard, played the final note properly, and handed it back with a kiss on his forehead.

Rae offered Nia a look at her bike before the next room. Nia said yes. I nearly volunteered a photographer. Shawna tightened her hand around mine until the thought passed safely through my body without becoming a purchase.

The hotel manager arrived carrying the financial statement. June leaned over to Dez. “Second war already got a casualty.” Dez looked at the total. “His deposit.” Nigga, the next campaign had begun before I'd finished enjoying the first truce.

## A Coalition Cannot Pay You in Exposure

“Nigga, why is your chair listed as a vehicle?” Tank asked.

The hotel manager had delivered the financial statement in a folder thick enough to qualify as supporting furniture. We had found the agenda, recovered the pen, and agreed to discuss money before the evening grew any more ceremonial. I had responded by taking my seat in a mechanical photo throne. Its footrest extended into the exact place the catering staff needed to walk. Even my sitting down had logistical consequences.

“It's powered,” I explained. “So is a vacuum,” Rae said. “One of those would help.” She had returned from showing Nia her bike and looked unusually pleased with a discussion of brake cables. Nia looked pleased too. Neither had submitted a report. I respected their privacy by waiting almost twelve seconds before suggesting a commemorative photograph. Shawna squeezed my shoulder until my interest in documentation subsided.

The second room offered strategy games, card battles, long role-playing stories, and enough imaginary governments to support my worst instincts. I had printed place cards for ministries. Rae's said Practical Affairs. Kit's said Cultural Affairs. Nia's said Legal Affairs. Shawna looked at the last word and asked whether her ministry could be Private Affairs, beginning with my immediate removal from public office. I assured her my domestic portfolio remained exceptionally strong. “Your portfolio was late to its appointment,” she said. Tank studied the invoice harder, out of respect for a man dying in office.

Velvet put her actual contract beside the ministries. She had a costume rack, a rehearsed number, and a fee that didn't become less real because I called the evening a coalition. Remy wanted his microphone checked and his fanfare left gloriously ridiculous. Mercedes wanted her own set and recording arrangements honored. Porsche wanted nobody borrowing her equipment in exchange for gratitude. Rosa wanted staff time paid. Those were concrete requests. My request concerned being photographed beneath a large symbolic eagle nobody remembered approving.

Mika loved the eagle. “It would look incredible over the stage.” I pointed at them triumphantly. “But we don't have the rigging or the money,” they continued. The betrayal arrived with professional measurements. They put their tiny model hotel on the table and began using coins to represent possible costs. It was the first casino activity that had frightened me before anybody placed a bet.

June and Dez arrived carrying the Blue Comet folder. The jacket came too, over Dez's arm. June identified it as her asset before she sat down. Dez identified her alterations as a long-term investment. Their 1967 peace arrangement had apparently failed because each believed the other had refused to sign. Both now wanted the current summit to recognize their excellent record of reasonable behavior. I understood the emotional appeal of a committee certifying whatever story made you look best.

Nia declined to certify either veteran's entire life. She would help read the old paper during the break. For now she wanted clear terms for this evening and then freedom to be a guest. Rae moved the good crackers within her reach without interrupting her sentence. Kit slid a lamp toward them, then reclaimed it an inch because she needed light on her own notes too. Nobody disappeared into service. Everybody kept a chair.

Dre sat down with his casserole and claimed the blue controller he'd brought. His Crip affiliation didn't make him my Minister of Blue Lighting, a position he declined before I finished explaining it. Darnell offered to underwrite entertainment from future yacht income. Velvet asked whether future money could arrive before present soundcheck. Darnell looked toward the bar, where his economic theory faced fewer follow-up questions.

I wanted to tell everyone that turn-based games meant a peaceful room. Shawna tapped the thick financial statement. “This waits while you think. Does it feel simple?” Fair. Waiting gave us time to understand decisions; it didn't remove the decisions. The useful game notes would remain plain, so a person could choose an appealing challenge without having me convert patience into a promise of ease.

I raised the ceremonial pen. Nia handed me an ordinary pencil. “Until we agree on the numbers.” The mechanical chair lowered itself with a squeak that sounded expensive. Tank caught my glass. Rosa moved the catering trolley past my newly humbled knees. Nigga, the treasury had opened for business, and its first order was getting my ass out of the aisle.

## P041 - Sid Meier's Civilization VI

### In one sentence

Build a civilization whose cities, discoveries, and relationships reflect your decisions, gradually creating a history with a direction of your own.

### What you do

Found a city, choose its production or research, and manage units, districts, policies, and relationships with neighboring powers over successive turns.

### How you play

Mouse / pointer | Usually waits for choices | Co-op details need checking

### Main catch

Solo turns allow deliberation, but menus and planning are heavy; test map gestures and readability rather than assuming cognitive simplicity.

### Edition considered

PC base game, no expansion requirement

### Editorial starting point

P041  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Build a civilization across a large sweep of history, choosing how cities grow, what people research and how to deal with neighboring powers. The appeal is seeing many small decisions create a society with a recognizable direction rather than following one prescribed storyline.

### The full catch

District placement, research, policies, diplomacy and multiple units produce heavy menu and planning demands. Single-player turns permit deliberation, but this is emphatically not cognitively simple because it is turn-based. Avoid assuming online turn settings match solo play; held map gestures and interface readability still need a trial.

### Try this first

Use the guided opening or a modest single-player start to found one city and make one production choice. Judge whether the explanations make that decision interesting before opening an empire's worth of additional responsibilities.

### Aiden at the summit

The Capital Has Four Fountains and No Change

Civilization VI encouraged me to describe the summit budget as an emerging nation. I pointed at the four decorative fountains on the rental sheet. “Public infrastructure.”

Rosa pointed at the unpaid extra staff hours. “Public embarrassment.” Tank leaned over the page. “Nigga, your civilization discovered waterfalls before wages.”

Kit wanted one fountain moved away from her music stand because its cheerful gurgling competed with every quiet note. Rae wanted the same fountain emptied before somebody knocked it over beside the signing table.

I argued that capitals needed grandeur. Nia asked whether grandeur had a receipt we could cancel. Mika admitted the fountains looked beautiful, then identified two we could return without dismantling half the room.

June offered to name the remaining pair after herself and Dez. Dez said naming something after her didn't satisfy a debt, especially if it mostly leaked.

We returned two fountains. The staff line became payable. I announced the first reform of my administration. Shawna wrote CARRIED THE FOUNTAIN beside my name, which was historically precise and politically devastating.

### Aiden’s verdict

The empire-building scope can be rewarding when its planning appeals; waiting turns do not simplify it. Our capital has achieved payroll by reducing its unnecessary population of fountains.

The Rabbids Have Applied for Cabinet Positions

Mario and the Rabbids formed an unlikely tactical team. Our summit's unlikely team was Kit and Tank, who wanted the same stage platform for completely different reasons.

Kit wanted height for karaoke. Tank wanted to see whether the buffet had been replenished without standing. “Strategic awareness,” he said. Nigga had studied my vocabulary too well.

## Both Sides of the Paper and Who Gets Paid to Hold It

Nia unfolded the old Blue Comet invoice during the break. June pointed at the front. “My signature. The other party refused.” Dez turned it over. “My signature. The other party refused.”

Nobody spoke for three beautiful seconds. Then Tank put his face in his hands.

“Niggas. Turn the fucking paper over.”

They had each spent fifty-nine years looking at the surface that supported their argument. June had signed the hall charge. Dez had signed the peace terms on the reverse. Both signatures were there, along with alternating jukebox selections, return of June's jacket before winter, and two ginger ales that had survived every retelling by remaining unmentioned.

I reached for my phone to photograph the breakthrough. Shawna said I could ask first. Both veterans agreed, provided I kept the picture out of any slideshow containing my face. Apparently they'd read the conditions of my hospitality more carefully than their own peace agreement.

June studied the jacket clause. Dez studied the ginger ales. Each had located a different obstacle to victory. Remy offered a two-sided fanfare. Velvet put a hand over his keyboard. “Let these women experience the silence, baby. They paid fifty-nine years for it.”

The present-day hotel invoice waited beside the historical one. Kit had found a duplicate lamp charge. Rae had found a labor line that assumed she'd remain available to repair furniture all evening. Nia had found herself listed as legal support through midnight. None of those entries had been agreed with the people whose time they described.

I said the hotel must have misunderstood. Rae turned the page toward me. The note read PER HOST REQUEST. My handwriting, for once, was entirely legible.

“Nigga, you can't call my hands a resource before you ask whether they're free.”

I began explaining that I'd meant available in case something went wrong. “Something already went wrong,” she said. “You spent my evening.” Her voice was sharper than it had been over the crackers, and it should have been. This wasn't a preference about olives. I had given somebody else a claim on her time because she had been helpful in front of me.

Kit said she could take some of the work. Rae shook her head. “The work isn't yours to redistribute either. Start with the assumption that I came to play.”

I saw Nia close her folder. She'd been trying to do that for twenty minutes. I had interpreted each new useful answer as an invitation to produce another question. A free lawyer was becoming one of my favorite features of the room, which was an ugly way to think about a woman who had come partly because she liked the mechanic sitting beside her.

I crossed out both assignments. The correction didn't make the earlier presumption clever. Nia kept the folder closed and said she would join the rest of the conversation as a person, which I considered a remarkably modest demand under the circumstances.

The sponsor approached before we could enjoy our breakthrough. He wanted a photograph with the coalition's respectable leadership before the performers changed into their show clothes. He nodded toward Kit and me, then looked at Velvet's headpiece as though it might damage his insurance.

Kit asked what he meant by respectable. He said polished, professional, welcoming to everyone. Velvet lifted her payment schedule. “I'm a professional. Welcoming everyone is already in the room. Which part of my head costs you customers?”

The man laughed because he wanted it to be a joke. It wasn't only a joke. Remy stood beside her in ordinary clothes, crown in hand, waiting to learn which version of him the sponsor considered sellable. Nobody at the table had volunteered to become the decorative proof that money could get along with difference if difference selected a quieter outfit.

I offered to take the photograph later. Shawna looked at me. “Later with whom?” I had tried delaying the choice without changing it. My skill at mediation often consisted of moving a bad sentence ten minutes into the future and hoping nobody followed.

The sponsor left to take a call. Kit exhaled. “I could do the picture and insist the show stays exactly as planned. It might keep the money uncomplicated.”

Rae looked at her. “Uncomplicated for whom?”

Kit was tired of that question, which didn't make it the wrong one. “For the people getting paid. Sometimes I've kept a library event alive by letting a donor feel like the room looked familiar. I'm not proud of every conversation. I also don't want the performers losing a fee because I chose the cleanest speech.”

Kit looked at me before continuing. “And don't decide the person who can write a check is the bravest one here. My library hours got cut. I can't replace a lost fee out of my account. That affects what risks feel available.” I had been preparing a generous expression; it became uncomfortable on my face. Rae nodded. “I believe you. It still matters whose face the sponsor chose for professional.” Kit said yes, both things mattered. Neither sentence paid the fee. We still had to find the money, and my advantages were about to become useful only if I stopped treating them as a superior moral personality.

Velvet nodded once. “That's a real problem. Here's my real answer: ask me before you purchase my survival with a smaller version of me.” She wasn't rejecting every negotiation. She wanted the person whose work was being negotiated to exist inside it. “I can choose an outfit for a client. I can also say the client's request costs more than the booking's worth. Don't make that choice and hand me the money like you rescued me.”

Remy said the sponsor had called his act surprisingly tasteful. “I know what he meant. I also know my act contains a pun about a royal accountant getting double-entry heartbreak. Tasteful wasn't a review. It was relief.”

Velvet laughed despite herself. “That joke is so fucking bad.” “And yet it belongs to me.” He put his crown on, crooked again. She left it crooked for once.

Rae described the hotel entrance earlier: Kit received a question about lighting, Rae received directions for contractors. Kit had initially explained the difference away because she hadn't wanted the room to become unpleasant before the party started. “I made the pleasant version more important than the thing you said happened,” Kit said now. Rae nodded. She didn't make Kit perform an apology twice just to prolong the advantage.

June leaned forward. “Money doesn't ask all of us to become respectable in the same way. But don't use that sentence to tell me I've never wanted a nice suit or a calm evening. I like both. This suit is beautiful.” Dez touched her sleeve. “It is. And this time it's actually on its owner.”

June let the laugh settle. “I've swallowed things at work to keep wages coming. I've also said no and worried afterward. I don't need my younger self put on trial by people who got to read the ending before deciding what she'd do.” She looked at me. “Your room needs choices. It doesn't need a purity competition sponsored by your wallet.”

I had been quietly imagining myself funding a perfect space where none of this occurred. That fantasy flattered the payer. It also made every complication somebody else's failure to appreciate the gift. I could rent chairs. I could pay staff. I couldn't make a Black woman's account of what happened at the door unnecessary just by paying for a nicer door.

Nia asked whether we could keep two questions visible: what immediate arrangement a person chose, and what conditions made the choice expensive. “I don't want my own compromises used to tell the next person they're obligated to make them. I also don't want a room full of spectators grading whether I resisted attractively enough.” Then she opened her hands. “That's my contribution. Somebody else can type it if they want it remembered.”

Mika typed. They also admitted they'd nearly accepted the sponsor's photograph request because they wanted the event to start and the room to look successful. “A beautiful room can photograph a problem out of existence,” they said. “I'm very good at that. I'd like to be good at knowing when I'm doing it.”

Kit asked about putting the cost somewhere visible. What would it take to keep the promised fees independent of the sponsor's flattering photograph? This time she asked Velvet first. Velvet named the amount already contracted, not a moral price. Rosa named the staffing balance. The hotel manager confirmed which duplicate and unopened rentals could be refunded. Numbers replaced the vague threat that honesty would bankrupt the evening.

Darnell arrived asking whether his party supplies qualified as entertainment expense. Tank glanced at the bag he'd been carrying. “Your cocaine is not a coalition department, nigga.” Darnell took it away and returned with a plate, where his contribution could remain the size of his appetite. We did not need his procurement story to understand the difference between an agreed fee and a personal decision.

I covered the contracted shortfall, approved the refunds, and told the sponsor the photograph would include whoever independently wanted to be in it. Nobody owed a performance of gratitude. He could choose whether he wanted the photograph on those terms. The room did not instantly become just. It became a room where one particular leverage attempt had failed without its target losing her fee.

Kit kept the duplicate-charge note. Rae kept her evening. Nia stayed seated instead of reopening the folder. June and Dez requested copies of both sides of their invoice and agreed to split the ancient ginger-ale debt symbolically over dinner. No interest. No tribunal. No commemorative eagle.

I offered the eagle at a discount. Shawna kissed my cheek, took my pencil, and said, “The survivors have suffered enough.” Then she asked me to dance later as her husband, without representing any ministry. Nigga, I accepted before somebody could turn the offer into a job description.

### Edition considered

PC Director's Cut

### Editorial starting point

P056  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Dragonfall brings Shadowrun's magic-and-technology world to Berlin and centers a crew with distinct personalities and histories. The Director's Cut expands the campaign and team material, making relationships and difficult loyalties a substantial reward for learning its tactical systems.

### The full catch

This remains a reading-heavy tactical RPG with character builds, equipment and team abilities. Its redesigned interface is not evidence that menus are few or self-explanatory. The standalone Director's Cut differs from the earlier expansion; complete timing, held gestures and late mission demands have not been verified here.

### Try this first

### Aiden at the summit

The Crew Has Conditions for Taking My Job

Dragonfall's crew had histories and loyalties. I recruited our own crew for a dangerous mission: persuade the hotel to refund the duplicate chair delivery. Everybody wanted to know the terms.

Rae wanted me present so I couldn't summarize the conversation afterward. Nia wanted a time limit on how long she'd spend helping. Kit wanted the promised lamp left untouched during the expedition.

Tank wanted food. Velvet wanted us back before her rehearsal. Remy wanted to perform his fanfare when we succeeded. We had not yet approached the manager and already possessed six competing victory conditions.

Shawna assembled the relevant receipts. She handed them to me, then made me read the first sentence of my own cancellation request aloud. It contained an apology and no mention of destiny.

The manager refunded the unopened chairs minus the stated fee. Rae accepted the result. Nia reclaimed her evening. Remy played two tasteful seconds before remembering his promise to be ridiculous and adding three gloriously unnecessary more.

Nigga, the crew had earned its ending. I had earned a smaller bill.

### Aiden’s verdict

The developed crew gives this campaign a strong personal draw, while its tactical and reading load remains. Our refund mission succeeded because every participant knew exactly what they wanted from it.

### Evidence desk

Inspected exact Director's Cut page confirms standalone identity, Berlin, expanded missions/team material and revised combat/interface. No all-path timing/hold guarantee; mature themes include explicit violence and difficult backstories.

### Aiden at the summit

The Matrix Password Is Under the Ice Bucket

Shadowrun's Hong Kong crew faced a dense world of intrigue. Our immediate intrigue concerned the sponsor's tablet, which contained the itemized charges and refused to open without a code.

I announced we would need a hacker. Mika lifted the ice bucket. The code was on a card beneath it. “We need a dry card.”

Nia read the charges while Rae held a napkin against the wet corner. Velvet found a proposed fee for using her stage name in a sponsor slideshow. She asked who had decided that was a benefit to her.

The sponsor called it promotional synergy. Remy made a sad little keyboard noise. Mercedes asked him to repeat it under the phrase, which improved the presentation enormously.

We removed the unapproved slide. Velvet offered a separate rate if the sponsor wanted her involvement. He declined, and everybody survived the absence of synergy.

I tried locking the tablet dramatically at the end. It played a cheerful confirmation sound. Nigga, our cyberpunk operation concluded like somebody successfully setting a kitchen timer.

### Aiden’s verdict

Battle Brothers' mercenary company attracted June. “Everybody signs before anybody carries anything,” she said. Dez raised an eyebrow. “Look at the Blue Comet discovering contracts.”

June and Dez inspected their two-sided copies of the 1967 agreement. Both signatures were undeniable now. June insisted signatures only mattered if promises were kept. Dez inspected the alternating-song clause and suggested June had spent fifty-nine years negotiating with the fucking jukebox.

Nigga, we had an alliance with conditions, which looked a lot like an ordinary agreement between people intending to remain friends after the evening cost money.

## P065 - Disgaea 5 Complete

### In one sentence

Enjoy an extravagant demonic rebellion where huge numbers and unusual combinations make increasingly elaborate systems part of the comedy and attraction.

### What you do

Try the opening move-and-act battle loop, then gradually explore jobs, items, special mechanics, and customization if those systems become enjoyable.

### How you play

Mixed controls | Usually waits for choices | Single-player; a friend can share the decisions

### Main catch

The Complete edition adds extensive material and deep systems; turn-based decisions do not make its menu or memory burden light.

### Edition considered

PC Complete edition

### Editorial starting point

P065  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Disgaea 5 turns tactical role-playing into an extravagant comic machine of demons, rebellion, huge numbers and unusual combinations. Its appeal is enjoying systems that become increasingly ridiculous, with a cast and world equally happy to push beyond ordinary fantasy restraint.

### The full catch

The Complete edition contains extensive added material and many deep systems: jobs, items, special battle mechanics and customization. That is a major menu and memory burden, not a promise of more effortless entertainment. Turn-based decisions help pacing, but the publisher's abundance is exactly the catch for someone wanting few systems.

### Try this first

Try only the opening explanation and a basic battle action. Leave bonus scenarios and long-term optimization alone until the fundamental move-and-act loop feels enjoyable; there is no requirement to consume everything included in the word Complete.

### Aiden at the summit

The Damage Number Is My Bar Estimate

Disgaea 5's glorious numerical excess made Remy read my event estimate like a battle result. He started with the chandelier line and increased his dramatic voice for every extra zero.

Velvet accompanied him with an increasingly horrified piano chord. Mercedes let her because the timing was excellent.

I said big numbers could represent big ambition. Rae found three separate charges for gold ribbon. “This nigga has dealt critical damage to stationery.” Kit corrected her that ribbon wasn't stationery, then admitted the distinction did not improve my defense.

Mika wanted one roll retained for the ceremony. They knew exactly where it would go. The other two could still be returned, which made their specific extravagance considerably more persuasive than my general one.

Nia marked the refund. Tank asked whether we could convert the savings into better dessert. Rosa said dessert was already good and he could stop campaigning before tasting it.

The damage report ended. Remy bowed. I survived with fewer ribbons and a numerical reputation that nobody intended to let me forget before breakfast.

### Aiden’s verdict

The exaggerated tactical systems can be a pleasure for someone who enjoys their depth, with dense menus understood. Our largest damage number belongs to a host repeatedly defeated by decorative ribbon.

### Evidence desk

Exact Complete listing documents included scenarios, jobs, customization and multiple strategic systems. Waits is tactical decision pacing; no full-path no-hold or low-menu claim is made.

## The Money Is Agreed and the Furniture Is Still an Argument

The financial sheet fit on one page when we stopped describing every expense as a historic investment. Performer payments. Staff time. Room charge. Equipment already in place. A small reserve for things that genuinely broke, distinct from things I became excited about while walking past a rental catalogue. Nia read the categories aloud. Rae checked the numbers against the receipts. Kit caught a duplicated lamp charge and looked so satisfied that I almost ordered a small trophy before remembering the entire fucking meeting.

Velvet received the confirmation she'd been waiting for. She put her phone away and became interested in the room again. Remy offered his arm. They went to check the microphone together, discussing a deliberately terrible pun he intended to put into the introduction. She said it was awful. He said that was its function. She agreed it performed its function flawlessly.

Rosa confirmed the additional staff time and went to speak with the kitchen. Mercedes and Porsche checked the recording schedule against the show order. Mika marked the approved equipment on the miniature floor plan, then looked at the actual doorway and frowned. The budget was intelligible. The rooms still required work. I had mistaken paying for square footage for knowing what to do with it, a confusion apparently common among niggas wearing ceremonial jackets indoors.

June and Dez kept their copied invoice in a plain envelope. Both sides. June wrote TURN OVER on the front in enormous letters. Dez wrote SAME TO YOU on the back. Their private jacket arrangement included looking for the old alteration pattern and having dinner afterward. The original jacket remained with Dez for the moment, which June permitted while describing herself as extraordinarily patient. Dez called this a promising new direction in historical fiction.

Nobody signed the final coalition charter. We had agreed financial terms, confirmed immediate payments, and recorded unresolved decorative claims for later review. I remained optimistic about those claims because optimism is cheap until you arrange a spotlight for it. Shawna read the little unresolved line, looked at me, and said nothing. Marriage contains silences with the tensile strength of steel.

Nia put the pen down. Rae asked whether she'd like a little air before the next room. Nia said yes before making it sound more considered. Kit handed them the room map, then noticed she'd given them her karaoke list instead. Everybody laughed, including Kit. She retrieved the list and told them the good balcony was marked on the actual map, which Mika still needed to verify. Even flirtation had encountered our venue problem.

I watched them leave and kept every helpful suggestion inside my own head. Shawna noticed. She linked her arm through mine. “You can learn.” I whispered that I possessed several advanced qualifications she hadn't examined tonight. “Then stop enrolling yourself in committees.” Her smile gave my future a much more interesting shape than the financial statement.

Tank carried the budget into the next room. Mika followed with the model hotel. June and Dez continued arguing fondly about whether alternating songs meant one each or whichever one sounded better. The Second Great War had survived its treasury meeting. Its armies now needed somewhere sensible to sit, and I was about to discover that a room could be expensive in ways a receipt didn't explain.
