## The Second Front Had Better Upholstery

The second front of the Great Butch versus Stud War opened when my welcome portrait jammed sideways in a doorway. Four grown people held the frame while I supervised from the angle where my face looked best.

"Nigga, move your face," Tank said.

"That's the back."

"It's still in the way."

Behind the portrait, Rae waited with a toolkit and a bag of crackers she considered beneath the summit's dignity. Kit, a white butch librarian, stood beside her holding three lighting diagrams and searching the top of her head for glasses already hanging from her collar. They had arrived to argue about rooms. I had given them an immediate common enemy with excellent dental work.

We had survived the financial negotiations. A provisional agenda existed. Nobody had signed the final charter, and Velvet Payroll could state the difference between an agreed performance fee and a host's vague promise without checking her notes. My casino convention floor now needed to become a place where people could spend an evening instead of a very expensive picture of one.

I had named the largest room the Chamber of Harmonious Victory. Shawna called it the ballroom because that was what the hotel sign said. She wanted us to finish the room survey, eat something sitting down, and eventually find a private stretch of evening where I was not addressing anyone in the plural.

Auntie June watched the portrait operation from a chair near the lift. At eighty-two, the retired bus driver had no interest in standing merely to observe my mistake from a greater height. Odessa, called Dez, sat beside her at eighty-four, wearing a jacket whose lining she had repaired herself. She had retired from sewing for customers, not from noticing bad workmanship.

"Blue Comet had narrower doors," June said.

"Blue Comet had fewer pictures of men blocking them," Dez answered.

They meant the entirely fictional social club where their entirely fictional 1967 feud had begun. Depending on who told it, the first war concerned a jukebox, a borrowed jacket, a missing quarter, or a look across a dance floor that neither woman described the same way twice. A peace agreement each called unsigned still existed on an old rental invoice. Dez carried it flat in her bag. June claimed to remember every clause, including several Dez insisted had never been written.

I had offered them honored positions as living witnesses. June asked whether witnesses got tea. Dez asked whether the honor included a chair with a cushion. Both demands had proved easier to satisfy than my plan for a heraldic balcony.

Mika unfolded the venue map on a table, then set one of their tiny model hotels beside it. They wanted the gala to begin before it became tomorrow's event. Unfortunately, they also wanted a floating courtyard display, a mirrored arch, and perhaps a little tower for the model hotel if nobody watched the budget too closely.

Nia joined Rae at the table. She was a Black trans lesbian and femme, belonged to overlapping caucuses, worked as a contract lawyer, and wrote so badly that her room preference looked like a threat against a staircase. She wanted a reasonable agreement and, less publicly, a dance with the woman now rejecting our crackers.

Remy wanted a clear microphone route for King Receipts. Velvet wanted dressing space and an entrance that did not require her to fold herself around a drinks cart. Mercedes wanted her keyboard near a socket. Porsche wanted a corner where she could hear Mercedes without listening to me describe the socket's strategic value.

"The labels aren't seating assignments," Nia said when I began dividing the map into heroic opposing territories. She moved her own place card beside Rae's, then visited Mika's model and asked about the courtyard. Her evening had already crossed three of my proposed borders.

Kit selected the lounge with the good light. Rae selected the table that did not wobble. June selected the tea. Dez selected the chair beside June, while making clear that this was geography and not surrender.

We tilted my portrait and finally got it through the doorway. Tank asked where to put it.

I pointed to the center of the map. Every head turned toward me.

Shawna took my hand and pointed instead to an empty patch of wall. For once, the winning maneuver required me to stand aside.

## P081 - Unpacking

### In one sentence

Discover a person's changing life through the belongings they keep, arrange and carry into new homes over the years.

### What you do

Open boxes, examine everyday objects and place them in rooms, noticing what each move reveals about their owner.

### How you play

Mouse / pointer | Usually waits for choices | Single-player; a friend can share the decisions

### Main catch

Small objects and visual searching still need checking, despite documented alternatives to holds, dragging and time limits.

### Edition considered

PC current release

### Editorial starting point

P081  /  A PLACE TO START

### Why it might click

Unpacking tells a life through belongings and the rooms they enter. The pleasure is partly arranging a space and partly noticing what survives each move. A familiar object can carry more character information than a long conversation. This is a worthwhile route for curiosity about people expressed through ordinary things.

### The full catch

The developer documents no time limits, mouse-only PC play and alternatives to dragging or holding. Those specific provisions make it a stronger starting candidate. Visual searching, small objects and deciding where things belong can still take effort. Check the Allow Items Anywhere option if placement rules interfere with the pleasure.

### Try this first

Open one box in the first room and place an object. Test the click-based interaction and whether the objects are comfortably visible before organizing everything.

### Aiden at the summit

Nobody Packed the Table Legs

Rae opened the summit's first relocation box and found three photographs of me, a champagne saber, and a velvet cushion labeled ESSENTIALS. The signing table was still leaning against the wall.

"Where are the legs?" she asked.

"Different department," I said. "This box contains leadership."

Shawna took the photographs out. Under them sat the little chipped bowl she always used for her earrings. I had packed it myself. She looked at me, then quietly put it on the windowsill.

Unpacking was on the screen, a life appearing through the belongings that kept coming along. Kit held up my saber and asked what recurring emotional truth required a sword at a seating meeting.

"Celebration, nigga."

Rae found the table legs inside my portrait crate. I had protected the picture with enough hardware to furnish a church. Shawna kept the bowl where she'd put it. My portraits went underneath the table, where they finally contributed to its stability.

### Aiden’s verdict

Rae accepts the room's arrangement provisionally. My portrait gets a supporting role beneath the table, while Shawna's chipped bowl secures the only windowsill nobody wants to fight over.

### Evidence desk

Steam supports belongings-as-story and no timers. Official developer accessibility page previously inspected supports mouse-only PC, no required holds/drags/simultaneous buttons and Allow Items Anywhere. Actual comfort remains individual.

### Why it might click

Townscaper is a construction toy in which clicks generate buildings and pleasing architectural connections. ### The full catch

The small tool set does not remove every physical task. Moving the view, zooming and placing a precise block may involve a different input pattern from selecting a menu. Preview those actions on the chosen device. This is a place-making activity with little authored character story, so the appeal must come from making rather than following a plot.

### Aiden at the summit

Mika Built a Hotel Nobody Could Enter

Mika watched Townscaper's buildings gather over water and began placing their tiny hotel models across our actual summit map. Within minutes the lesbian caucus occupied a charming waterfront district with no bridge.

"It looks spectacular," they said.

"It looks stranded," Rae said, balancing a cheese plate above the model harbor. "Where do the snacks cross?"

I offered a gondola. Velvet asked whether the gondolier's wages were inside the newly agreed budget. I offered a smaller gondola.

Kit moved one miniature tower and opened a direct path from the entrance to the lounge. Mika stared at the gap as if she had knocked out a beautiful tooth.

Then Nia put two tiny chairs beside the water and asked Rae whether this imaginary neighborhood had a late bar.

Rae moved her cheese plate closer. Mika gave the bar a roof terrace. The map acquired a passage, a date venue, and precisely one less monument to my judgment.

### Aiden’s verdict

Mika keeps the waterfront, Kit keeps the open path, and Rae keeps the cheese. I withdraw the gondola proposal after discovering a boat cannot be paid in atmosphere.

The Roof Delegation Came Back Hungry

Halfway there, Rosa stopped beside a little balcony. Somebody had put two chairs in the shade. Music drifted up from the courtyard. She sat.

"The summit's above us," I said.

"So is the sun. I'm not chasing that either."

## P090 - Lil Gator Game

### In one sentence

Turn a friendly island into a make-believe adventure, meeting characters and enjoying the playful possibilities of its ordinary spaces.

### What you do

Explore the island, talk with characters and take part in activities involving movement, climbing and improvised adventure.

### How you play

Movement + camera | Timing needs checking | Single-player; a friend can share the decisions

### Main catch

Jumping, climbing, gliding and camera coordination are meaningful demands; the friendly tone does not remove them.

### Edition considered

PC release

### Editorial starting point

P090  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Lil Gator Game builds an island adventure around play, make-believe and meeting people who can become part of it. Exploration and small activities offer a lighthearted sense of progress. The emotional question of sharing an enthusiasm may resonate even when the visual style is deliberately playful.

### The full catch

This remains a movement-based adventure. Check camera control, climbing, gliding, jumping and the frequency of held or combined inputs in the chosen version. A playful tone does not make those demands disappear. Someone who wants a darker mystery or dense adult dialogue may simply prefer another shelf, which is a matter of taste.

### Try this first

Explore one nearby patch of the opening area and talk to a character. Try the basic movement and camera separately before committing to traversal challenges.

### Aiden at the summit

The Cardboard Kingdom Asked for a Quiet Room

Remy made a cardboard crown for the room-allocation contest. Then he made one for Velvet, who objected to the fit, improved it with a silver napkin, and immediately claimed the lounge.

Lil Gator Game's make-believe adventure gave my competitive instincts terrible encouragement. I declared the corridor an unexplored kingdom and challenged Kit to seize it.

She walked past me carrying her tea.

"You surrender?"

"I'm going somewhere I can hear myself."

That left me king of a corridor with no subjects. Rae joined Kit. Nia followed with two cushions. Their quiet-room proposal suddenly had more members than my conquest.

Remy folded his cardboard sword into a sign pointing toward them. Velvet donated the silver napkin as a flag, then returned to demand actual stage time.

I brought the remaining crowns to the quiet room. Shawna chose one, put it on me crooked, and asked whether a king could sit still for five minutes.

I began a historically peaceful reign.

### Aiden’s verdict

The cardboard kingdom retains its costumes but acquires a quiet room. My reign is limited to one chair, five minutes, and whatever Shawna considers acceptable royal fidgeting.

## The Same Door Did Not Look the Same from Every Chair

June offered to guide the room survey because she had driven a bus through worse arrangements than my hotel corridor. Dez said one of those arrangements had included a flowerpot that never recovered.

"The flowerpot was in the road."

"It was beside the road."

"It came to a very final understanding of beside."

I asked whether the Blue Comet peace agreement covered this incident. Both women told me it happened later. Even an imaginary war possessed boundaries I was capable of misunderstanding.

We started at the entrance. Kit carried the map. Rae carried the good crackers. Nia volunteered to carry the napkins, then forgot them on the table because Rae had taken off her jacket and apparently created an administrative distraction.

The first disagreement concerned a chair.

Kit wanted the quiet-room chair near the window. Rae wanted it turned slightly so the door remained visible. Mika tried the angle. Kit moved it back.

"The light's better here."

"I can see the light from the other angle," Rae said.

"You could stop watching the door for one evening."

The room went still in a way none of my rented acoustic panels had achieved.

Kit's hand stayed on the chair. She was white, butch, soft-spoken until a matter of lighting or music made softness inconvenient. Rae was a Black stud who repaired bicycles, liked a good mystery, and had spent the afternoon making our furniture behave. At that moment, neither needed me to turn her into a delegation summary.

Rae set down the crackers.

"Was that a suggestion or something you decided I ought to learn?"

Kit looked at the chair, then at her. "A suggestion. Badly put."

"Nigga, you said it like I was doing the evening wrong."

I stepped forward with the authority of a man who had bought the room. Nia held out the forgotten napkins.

"Could you get these?"

I got them. My contribution improved immediately.

Kit said she watched doors too. She had stories about being mistaken for someone else, challenged in bathrooms, and studied by men who thought a haircut gave them permission to ask questions. She started telling one, then stopped herself before Rae had to stop her.

"That doesn't mean I know what you were doing."

"I was choosing a chair."

"Right."

"And yes, I wanted the door where I could see it. You don't get my whole life for the price of moving a lamp."

Kit moved the lamp.

Rae watched the new light reach the page. "You do make a room look good. I noticed. I just want a say in where I am inside it."

Kit nodded. "Your table repair made my whole drawing possible. I could have remembered that before treating you like part of the furniture."

June remained in the doorway with one hand on Dez's bag. "I like seeing the door too. Sometimes it's because I'm old and waiting for the tea. Sometimes it isn't. Folks can ask before they finish the story."

She was a Black butch, a fact that made my earlier idea of assigning white butches one territory and Black studs another look even stupider in retrospect. June had been herself before Kit was born, and no neat diagram was going to reorganize her for my convenience.

"I wasn't trying to make it racial," Kit said, then winced at her own sentence.

Rae leaned against the table. "You don't have to be trying for it to be in the room."

The distinction sat there. Nobody applauded. Velvet looked at her watch, then put it away. She had a rehearsal to reach, but she also knew when a room had to finish the conversation it had started.

Nia took the crackers from Rae's hand and ate one.

"I have a selfish question. If we put the chair at your angle, where do I sit?"

Rae pointed beside it.

"Oh. Excellent."

Kit laughed once, relieved, then did not mistake the laugh for permission to skip the awkward part.

"Would you tell me if I'm doing that again?"

"I might. I might also go get a drink. I'm not promising to supervise you."

"Fair."

They tested the chair at the new angle. The lamp still worked.

That ought to have been enough for me to carry away. Instead, I offered to make the entire hotel corridor private so nobody would have to deal with strangers.

Mika looked at the cost sheet as if it had just threatened their family.

Rae looked at me. "I didn't ask you to buy the street."

"Not the street. Just a very affordable section of indoors."

Shawna folded her arms. "You think every problem ends where your reservation begins."

I wanted to disagree. My card was already halfway out of my pocket, which weakened the defense.

June said driving a bus had taught her to notice who felt entitled to explain the route to her while she was driving it. She also said some of her best passengers had been the ones who brought gossip and left her to do her job. She refused to turn decades of people into one moral photograph for my summit.

"Some folks were trouble. Some were funny. One man brought me a peach every Tuesday and never once tried to own the conversation."

Dez snorted. "You flirted with that man."

"He brought excellent peaches."

"Did you want him?"

"I wanted the peaches. You kept eating them."

Rae laughed, and the room could breathe again without pretending the earlier exchange had disappeared.

Kit said she disliked being read as an imitation of a man. Rae said that happened to her too, but they did not always get the same imitation assigned to them. She remembered one stranger calling her threatening while treating her white companion's matching boots as stylish.

"This one stranger," she said when I reached for my notes. "Don't turn me into your survey."

I closed the notebook.

Nia asked whether Rae wanted her nearby when a moment like that happened, or whether stepping in made the scene bigger. Rae considered it instead of supplying the perfect romantic answer.

"Ask me. Sometimes stand beside me. Sometimes let me finish. And don't start a courtroom because somebody looked at us."

Nia nodded. "I can resist one courtroom."

"Try two."

Their joking had a little edge. Nia's professional competence was not a key to every locked part of Rae's evening. Rae's alertness was not a command that Nia spend the night monitoring her. They were finding a way to want each other's company without converting care into a permanent assignment.

Kit sat on the other chair and admitted she had liked being the practical one in our room argument. She had mistaken being useful for being right about everybody else's comfort.

"Nigga, welcome to my entire personality," I said.

Shawna patted my shoulder. "You're visiting practicality. Don't buy property yet."

Mika asked what should change on the actual map. It was a good question because it gave the conversation somewhere to land besides my growing collection of important phrases.

We kept two chair positions available. Nobody had to explain choosing either. The quiet room stayed optional. The information sign named a person to ask for help without promising that a rented convention floor could guarantee every encounter beyond it.

Velvet wanted the route to her dressing room clear so she could enter without inviting an audience to inspect her while she was half ready. Remy wanted the same courtesy with his stage clothes. June wanted tea in a cup she could hold comfortably. Dez wanted a cushion that did not slide every time she turned to argue.

These were requests from particular people. They did not cancel the difficult conversation. They made it possible to do something with it.

Tank asked Rae whether she wanted company when she returned to the reception desk to check the room key. He managed to ask it without already standing in front of her.

"Maybe later," she said. "I want to finish this tea."

He sat down. The bread stayed within her reach. For a man who could block a doorway by existing in it, he had a surprisingly good understanding of when not to become a wall.

Kit picked up the map again, then paused at the door.

"Rae, do you want to finish this route now?"

"In a minute."

Kit waited. Nia stayed beside the angled chair. I took Shawna's hand and resisted my final temptation to announce that the room had reached a historic understanding.

Tank arrived with tea before I could relapse.

June accepted her cup. Dez took the other chair, still claiming the flowerpot had been perfectly innocent. Outside the window, strangers crossed the courtyard without knowing our stories, our titles, or what the chairs had cost. We could not write their thoughts into the venue annex.

We could stop pretending everybody inside the room had entered it by the same route.

## P091 - Smushi Come Home

### In one sentence

Help a tiny mushroom find a way home through a forest whose scale makes ordinary places feel like an adventure.

### What you do

Explore the forest, meet characters and try traversal activities while following the mushroom's journey toward a familiar home.

### How you play

Movement + camera | Timing needs checking | Single-player; a friend can share the decisions

### Main catch

Movement holds, jumps and camera control need checking, especially before relying on its small scale as evidence of simplicity.

### Edition considered

PC release

### Editorial starting point

P091  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Smushi Come Home follows a tiny mushroom trying to return home through a forest. New tools, helpful creatures and light puzzles give the trip a clear purpose. The small scale can make familiar natural objects feel surprising, and the mycology journal supplies another kind of curiosity beyond simply reaching the next place.

### The full catch

The primary description explicitly includes running, gliding, climbing, swimming and light platforming. Those are real control demands despite the cozy presentation. Assess held movement, steering and transitions between abilities. An own-pace exploration claim does not demonstrate that every jump or required action will be comfortable.

### Try this first

Try a small stretch of walking and one conversation. Then inspect the earliest necessary traversal action before deciding whether the homeward journey feels inviting.

### Aiden at the summit

The Smallest Delegate Had the Largest Sign

Mika placed a tiny model guest beside the venue map to demonstrate scale. Smushi Come Home was on the screen, a mushroom making a forest feel enormous. The model guest vanished beneath my ceremonial nameplate.

"That's a realistic representation," Rae said. "Nobody can see around your ass."

I shortened the nameplate by removing FOUNDER OF EXCELLENCE. It still covered the lounge.

Kit took the little figure on a tour between our model furniture. Three corners trapped it. One proposed doorway led directly into a decorative hedge. The hedge had cost me more than my first car.

Velvet picked it up and wore it briefly as a collar.

"Now it has a career."

Mika drew a clearer route. Remy carried the tiny guest to the model stage and made it bow. Nia asked whether this miniature person could reach the signing table.

Rae lowered the model pedestal. For the first time, the smallest delegate could see the room without climbing my reputation.

### Aiden’s verdict

The miniature guest survives the inspection and reaches the table. Velvet acquires a hedge collar, while FOUNDER OF EXCELLENCE becomes spare lettering for a considerably smaller sign.

### How you play

### Why it might click

Haven Park combines a small explorable park with campsite improvements and conversations. Taking care of a place gives wandering a practical rhythm: find something, learn what a visitor needs and make the park more welcoming. Its family connection and local stories provide a modest narrative thread around that activity.

### The full catch

The developer presents a peaceful open world, but building and gathering still introduce resources, quests and navigation. Check camera behavior, interaction distance, held movement and how many unfinished tasks the interface expects you to track. ### Aiden at the summit

The Campground Had Better Hospitality Than My Summit

Haven Park turned improving a campsite into a persuasive argument against my lounge. Mine had six velvet ropes, four ornamental lamps, and nowhere to put a cup.

Tank solved the cup problem by holding everybody's drinks until Rosa caught him trying to scratch his nose.

"Nigga, you're becoming furniture."

Rae wanted a solid table. Kit wanted a lamp that illuminated something besides its own price. Nia wanted the chair beside Rae, but called it a review of seating continuity.

Mika arranged a small corner with everything requested. People moved into it before I finished explaining the superior atmosphere near the ropes.

Velvet sat in my grandest chair, put her feet on its matching ottoman, and announced she would use the abandoned luxury suite as a dressing area.

I said the suite was technically a corner.

"Then you finally priced a corner correctly."

Shawna brought me to the useful little campsite. Tank could scratch his nose again.

### Aiden’s verdict

The improved corner receives a table, sensible light, and voluntary company. Velvet claims the deserted luxury furniture for costume changes, a use that finally justifies its dramatic upholstery.

## P093 - Mail Time

### In one sentence

Make little deliveries through a storybook forest, with meeting people along the route providing much of the charm and interest.

Travel through the forest, speak with characters and carry letters or requests between the people you encounter there.

### How you play

Movement + camera | Some real-time demands | Single-player; a friend can share the decisions

### Main catch

Platforming, jumping, gliding and remembering destinations can complicate the otherwise gentle delivery premise.

### Edition considered

PC release

### Editorial starting point

P093  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Mail Time turns deliveries into a forest adventure with distinct characters and places. Letters provide a clear reason to visit someone, while the world makes the route part of the attraction. It is a potential option for enjoying small social encounters without needing a dense mystery or a complicated economic simulation.

### The full catch

The developer explicitly states no time limits or fall damage, which supports the pace side of this candidate. It also explicitly includes running, jumping and gliding. These physical demands must be assessed separately. Check camera movement, held glide input and remembering delivery destinations; do not assume the listed accessibility options solve every concern.

### Try this first

Follow one early delivery from address to recipient. Test the first necessary jump or glide at a comfortable moment before planning a full mail route.

### Aiden at the summit

The Letter Took the Scenic Route

Nia wrote Rae a note and asked me to deliver it while Mail Time sent its small courier through a forest full of encounters.

I was an excellent choice. Charming, recognizable, impossible to ignore.

I carried the envelope to Kit, who directed me past the model hotel. Mika stopped me to relocate a doorway. Velvet wanted to know why her dressing room had become a public shortcut. Tank needed help lifting a tray.

By the time I found Rae, she and Nia were sharing a lemonade.

"Nigga, the author got here first." "The courier investigated the route."

Nia read the envelope and frowned. I had brought the wrong one. This contained her beautifully reasoned objection to the hotel surcharge, written so badly Rae thought it was a romantic threat against a coat rack.

Rae tucked it into her jacket anyway.

"First thing you ever gave me in writing."

Nia laughed, reached for another envelope, and handled her own distribution.

### Aiden’s verdict

The courier is relieved of romantic correspondence but retained for lifting trays. Rae keeps the surcharge objection, whose terrible handwriting has accidentally made it more personal than intended.

## P094 - Lake

### In one sentence

Follow a familiar delivery route through a lakeside community, getting to know people through workday conversations and personal choices.

### What you do

Drive the mail truck, make deliveries and talk with residents, deciding how you want to spend time with them.

### How you play

Movement + camera | Timing needs checking | Single-player; a friend can share the decisions

### Main catch

Driving and walking controls are central; camera coordination, menus and particular sequences still need checking.

### Edition considered

PC base game

### Editorial starting point

P094  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Lake follows Meredith during a return to her hometown and a temporary job delivering mail. Adult relationships, ordinary decisions and the question of what kind of life to choose are the main attractions. The setting offers a slower social story rather than a grand fantasy quest.

### The full catch

Driving and walking are real activities, not just scenery between dialogue screens. The developer mentions an autopilot option for the mail truck, which is worth checking, but it does not establish that all navigation becomes automatic. Verify camera control, interaction and the extent of that feature in the exact release before relying on it.

### Try this first

Try one nearby delivery and conversation. Examine the driving assistance option, then decide whether the route itself adds pleasure or merely gets between the conversations.

### Aiden at the summit

Meredith Got Mail, I Got Room Service

Lake's temporary return to hometown routines made Shawna ask what I would do if I had one ordinary day without arranging a spectacle.

"Spend it with you." "Doing what?"

I opened my mouth and almost rented a yacht.

She caught it. "Try smaller."

We took a cart of summit room notices along the corridor. She knocked; I handed over envelopes. Kit invited us in to hear two competing entrance songs. Velvet sent us away with a costume hook to return. Remy asked whether we could leave his flowers outside Nia's room for safekeeping. They were for his own date later.

The small deliveries kept becoming conversations. Nobody needed me to proclaim anything. I disliked how good it felt.

At the last door, Shawna ordered sandwiches and changed our room notice from HOST AVAILABLE to BACK LATER.

"Nigga," I said, "that's a major constitutional amendment."

She kissed me and shut the door on my speech.

### Aiden’s verdict

The host takes an ordinary break with his wife. Delivery notices remain legible, flowers reach safekeeping, and the coalition survives two sandwiches without appointing an acting supreme commander.

### Why it might click

SEASON centers a bicycle journey, a customizable journal and the effort to preserve memories of a changing world. ### The full catch

A reflective premise does not establish an easy physical route. Cycling, walking, camera use and arranging journal material are different interactions to check. ### Aiden at the summit

The Future Requested Fewer Selfies

I announced a summit time capsule after seeing SEASON turn travel, recordings, and a journal into a way of remembering a changing world. My first proposed contents were photographs of me opening things.

Rosa suggested something somebody might miss.

Kit recorded the entrance music she and Remy were still arguing over. June recorded her account of the Blue Comet jukebox. Dez immediately requested an opposing track. Nia wrote down a joke Rae had made, then crossed out a sentence nobody else got to read.

Mika photographed their tiny hotel before the rooms changed again.

Darnell offered a recording of his yacht pitch. Mercedes pressed stop before he reached the second deck.

"Nigga, the future's suffered enough."

Shawna took my camera and filmed everybody passing dishes around the table. I appeared for three seconds, looking for her.

"That's all I get?" "That's what you were doing."

I kept that clip twice, once in the capsule and once where I could find it without a committee.

### Aiden’s verdict

The future receives a repaired cart, imperfect music, and a table full of people. Darnell's yacht presentation is excluded for length; my three seconds receive a private backup.

The developer's description includes a hoverbike, climbing, jumping and gliding. Navigation and held movement therefore deserve a practical trial. ## Velvet Declared the Dressing Room Sovereign

The middle of the room survey became a border dispute when I suggested visitors could pass through Velvet's dressing area on their way to the balcony.

She looked at me through the mirror. One earring was on. One lay beside the brush. Her expression did not need the second earring to become complete.

"It'll cost you a show."

Mika examined the alternative path. It was perfectly usable. It passed a window, a water jug, and a chair Kit had already claimed for the interval before karaoke. The only genuine obstacle was my desire for the map to look symmetrical.

Rae erased the shortcut. Nia wrote PRIVATE beside the dressing room, badly enough that Remy asked whether it said PIRATE. Velvet considered the latter for a second, then requested both accurate spelling and a working door latch.

June remembered a dressing corner at the Blue Comet made private by a coat hung across two chairs. Dez said she had been wearing the coat. June said that was precisely why everybody remembered it.

Nobody attempted to solve the old ownership claim. Kit checked the current latch. It worked. Mika placed the water jug outside the alternate route so people could stop without crowding the doorway.

I apologized to Velvet. She accepted the apology and asked me to carry the spare chair. I performed this task with the gravity of a man repairing an international incident through furniture.

When I returned, Remy was testing the stage approach. He knocked before entering the dressing space to ask about the shared mirror. Velvet invited him in. They made their own arrangement in thirty seconds.

Shawna watched me calculate how many diagrams I had produced to avoid that simple conversation.

"Don't say it," I told her.

"I wasn't going to."

That was worse. She smiled, took the map from my hand, and wrote OUR BREAK beside the courtyard. No border, no flag, just two words that gave me a destination worth defending.

The room began changing. Kit put out a library book she had borrowed for the trip. Remy set his flowers in water. Rosa moved two chairs together without explaining who would use them.

Velvet insisted the room could also hold people who did not want to give a family presentation. Nia nodded and placed blank cards beside the photographs rather than labels beneath anybody's seat.

I removed the cushion picture myself. Shawna kept one wedding photo near the door, where I could see both of us in it instead of just my spectacular jacket.

### Aiden’s verdict

The family lounge becomes a room for people with different histories, including private ones. One wedding picture stays, while fourteen host portraits face a difficult but overdue housing shortage.

## The Blue Comet Had Never Owned the Whole Sky

Darnell appeared on the balcony with a proposal to sponsor its naming rights. He offered a yacht photograph, an anecdote nobody had requested, and a bag of party baggage he wisely kept away from the tea.

Mercedes asked what he meant by sponsor.

"Exposure."

"Nigga, we're already outside."

He tried again with the word partnership. Velvet asked for a number. The discussion ended when no number appeared.

Below us, the courtyard lights had come on. Kit wanted one brighter patch near the path. Mika wanted the reflections to remain soft. They tried two settings and found a third both liked. I was preparing to call this a triumph of coalition procedure when June asked whether anybody could simply enjoy it for a minute.

We did.

Dez took out the Blue Comet scrapbook. A photograph showed the two women much younger, standing beneath a sign whose paint had already begun to peel. June wore the disputed jacket. Dez's hand was caught at its sleeve.

I asked who owned it at the moment of the photograph.

"The person wearing it," June said.

"The person foolish enough to lend it," Dez said.

Rae leaned in to look, then passed the book to Nia. Nobody asked the photograph to settle the dispute. It was doing another job: keeping an evening visible after the room itself was gone.

Shawna rested her head against my shoulder. I considered all the money I had spent trying to produce a moment that looked like this, then tried very hard not to announce that thought and ruin the free version.

Mika marked the balcony as an optional stop with chairs, water, and enough light to find the way back. Darnell wanted his name on the mark. Mercedes drew a little star instead.

"Nigga, that's exposure," she told him.

He laughed despite himself. June closed the scrapbook. Dez kept one hand on it. The sky remained completely indifferent to our naming rights, which made it the only venue feature I had no chance of accidentally renting.

Observation of the environment supplies information that later becomes meaningful, making discovery feel like learning a place rather than completing disconnected puzzles. The 2024 remake expands and reimagines the original game's world.

### The full catch

The remake explicitly uses free movement in a three-dimensional environment. That matters for camera comfort and must not be confused with the 1997 original's screen navigation. Its interlocking clues also make memory and note-taking significant. This is a deliberate reasoning stretch, not an easy label earned by the absence of a weapon.

Kit's symbols survive alongside plain labels, and the storage room returns to storage. Remy finds his destination with enough confidence to celebrate at a volume the corridor can tolerate.

## The Annex Was Agreed, the Evening Was Still Ours

We spread the revised venue plan across the table Rae had made stable. It no longer looked like a campaign map drawn by a man expecting his portrait to repel invaders.

The ballroom had a clear entrance. The quiet room had a working lamp and no compulsory activity. Velvet's dressing area had a proper boundary. The courtyard had real hours, seats, and a route back inside when the evening moved on. The snacks could be reached without solving a decorative problem.

Kit traced the paths once with her finger. Mika checked the room names against the hotel signs. Remy set his microphone case beside the agreed stage position and found that his own feet still had somewhere to go.

"Nigga," Tank said, "we built walking."

"We negotiated an annex."

"We negotiated walking with snacks."

Nia read the agreement aloud in ordinary language. She had crossed out one of my phrases, sovereign corridor of collective splendor, and replaced it with clear passage. I privately mourned the phrase, which had cost nothing and still managed to be wasteful.

Rae asked whether people could change rooms when they wanted. Yes. Whether the quiet room required an explanation. No. Whether somebody could keep watching a game instead of joining the next ceremony rehearsal. Yes.

These answers sounded so ordinary that I nearly missed how much work my original plan had made necessary.

June took the pencil and marked the annex approved. Dez marked it too, then pointed at the old Blue Comet paper beside it.

"Separate question."

June nodded. "Still separate."

The final charter remained unsigned. The agreement from 1967 remained, in each veteran's account, unsigned by the other. We had settled where to sit without pretending to settle every story people brought into the room. Even I could see the difference, though it annoyed my desire for a dramatic concluding photograph.

Velvet folded the map and asked when the actual stage would be ready. Mika looked toward the costume racks, the unopened equipment cases, and the enormous box I had not yet explained.

"What is that?" Shawna asked.

"A mechanism."

"For what?"

I gave an answer containing the words seamless, immersive, and reveal. Rae picked up her toolkit again. Kit found her glasses. Remy began humming a fanfare designed to make any forthcoming embarrassment sound official.

Before we moved on, Nia touched Rae's elbow and asked whether the courtyard still had time for a dance later. Rae said yes. Nothing was signed, nobody applauded, and the answer looked stronger for not being announced.

Shawna led me through the clear passage we had finally managed to create. She stopped at the window, took my face in her hands, and kissed me until I forgot to assess the square footage.

Then she pointed at the box.

"Come on, nigga. Let's find out what you bought."

The next front of the war was waiting inside, probably with assembly instructions I had mistaken for optional reading.

## The Battle of the Unassembled Stage

The mechanism inside my enormous box was a curtain opener with no curtain, a revolving stand with no assigned purpose, and a gold lever so impressive it distracted me from both omissions.

Rae put the delivery sheet on the table. "Which thing does the useful thing?"

I pointed at the lever.

She lifted it. Nothing happened anywhere else.

Tank nodded. "Portable authority, nigga."

Our venue annex was settled. People knew where the rooms were, the quiet space had a working lamp, and Velvet's dressing area no longer doubled as a shortcut for my sense of symmetry. All that remained was to build a ceremony capable of holding the people, the paper, the costumes, and my deteriorating confidence without collapsing under any of them.

I had prepared for this task by ordering objects.

Mika had prepared by measuring. This gave them an unfair advantage the moment we began. They placed their tiny hotel model on a clear patch of table, laid out the agreed route, and asked us to stop adding towers until the actual furniture worked.

Kit, the white butch librarian, carried the lighting plan under one arm and searched for her glasses with the other hand. They were in her jacket pocket. Remy discovered them while looking for the microphone clip, received a grateful smile, and ruined it with a pun about seeing eye to eye. Kit laughed anyway, which encouraged him beyond the interests of the room.

Velvet arrived wearing half her performance costume and carrying the other half in a bag large enough to contain a small successful business. She wanted a clear turn beside the stage, a usable mirror, and the fee we had already agreed. Her budget instincts were sharper than my scissors, and considerably more likely to cut something.

Rae wanted the signing table to stand still. This had become her recurring demand because I had repeatedly purchased things that photographed better than they supported elbows. Nia wanted that table near the room, where people could speak without being exhibited like auction lots. She also wanted to ask Rae about the dance, but every time she approached, somebody handed her another page written in my decorative language.

Auntie June and Dez took their chairs near the rehearsal area. June wore the posture of a retired bus driver who could still tell when somebody had parked badly from across a room. Dez wore June's old jacket, repaired so carefully that its disputed ownership had survived longer than many actual institutions.

Between them lay the Blue Comet rental invoice. The peace terms were on its back. June had signed the front and Dez the back, an arrangement that had supported fifty-nine years of each declaring the other's signature absent. I had initially treated this as a tragedy of diplomacy. Shawna said it sounded like two women who enjoyed having an excuse to bring up the same night.

The first Great Butch versus Stud War belonged to our invented 1967 social club history, complete with contradictory jukebox accounts and an unreasonable quantity of emotional investment in one borrowed jacket. The second had reached the stage-equipment phase. Nobody's dignity required a vote. My purchases, unfortunately, required several.

I proposed raising the signing table on a platform beneath the illuminated portrait. Rae sat at the table and asked me to hand her the pen. I had to walk around a vase, a costume rack, and the unconnected lever to reach her.

"Nigga," she said, "we have discovered the problem."

Mika moved the vase. Kit moved the rack. I held the lever because nobody had yet found it a job. Shawna put a small ordinary pen in my other hand and guided me back along the clear route.

"Try this version."

I handed the pen to Rae. She wrote a test word, pushed gently against the table, and looked up. It wobbled.

Tank took the lever from me. For one terrible second I thought he had discovered its purpose. Then he set it aside and helped Rae inspect the legs.

The war had finally found its first objective: a table that could survive somebody agreeing with somebody else.

## Dez Refused to Let the Jacket Lose on a Technicality

The costume rehearsal stopped when June noticed a loose thread at Dez's cuff. She reached for it. Dez caught her wrist gently.

"Leave it. You'll make it worse."

"I drove a bus full of people through winter. I can manage a thread."

"That's why I never let the bus hem my clothes."

Rae laughed into her drink. Nia tried not to, failed, and ended up holding the glass while Rae found a small sewing kit. Dez accepted the kit with the calm of somebody returning to familiar tools. June stayed beside her despite having several strong opinions about being supervised.

The jacket lay across both their knees. It had belonged to June first. It had spent enough time with Dez that every repair was also a small account of where it had been. Neither woman needed me to explain this, so naturally I began.

Shawna put a sandwich in my mouth.

Dez repaired the cuff. June held the little lamp at a useful angle without commenting on the appointment. Velvet came over to inspect the work and asked whether Dez would look at a loose fastening on her costume.

"For you, yes."

I offered to make the work an official heritage demonstration. Dez told me to finish chewing.

The repairs were small, exact, and almost invisible when done. They made the clothes behave better without making their wearers into examples of anything. Remy tried his stage turn nearby. Kit adjusted the light and accidentally directed it into my eyes, which everybody regarded as an acceptable temporary arrangement.

When Dez handed the jacket back to June, the room went quiet for one beat. June inspected the cuff, nodded, and helped Dez put it on again.

"There," she said.

"About time you returned it," Dez answered.

The old argument resumed before I could declare peace. Nia laughed properly this time, and Rae looked at her as if the sound had improved the room.

Mika called us back to the rehearsal route. The table still needed checking, the curtain still needed its final position, and the jacket had won the right to keep going without a plaque.

## The Camera Did Not Get to Name Everybody

The photographer arrived during the costume check and asked where he should put the men.

Remy raised one hand. Tank raised a bread roll. I stepped into the best light on instinct.

The photographer pointed at Velvet, Kit, and Rae.

"Also you three. The masculine side of the group."

Velvet looked down at her silver costume, then back at him.

"Baby, if this is your idea of masculine, I need to see what you wore to work yesterday."

His name was Owen. He was an adult gay man hired by the hotel, which he told us immediately, as if the information might excuse the photograph before he took it. It did not make him a villain. It also did not arrange anybody's feet.

"I meant the presentation," he said.

"Then ask about the picture you want," Remy said. "Don't assign people a whole life to get a balanced triangle."

I offered to form the triangle around myself. Shawna moved me two feet to the left and improved the conversation.

Owen lowered the camera and claimed he had meant to separate sharp tailoring from flowing costumes. Velvet looked down at the dress he had put on the tailored side. Even his excuse needed rearranging.

Kit considered the new proposal. She was willing to stand beside the silver costume. Rae wanted to remain beside Nia. Velvet wanted the light slightly higher. Remy wanted his name used when he was not performing.

These requests did not require a tribunal. Owen listened, adjusted, and began again.

The fees were already protected by the earlier budget argument. I thought that meant the photograph would be easy. Then the hotel's sponsorship coordinator arrived with an opinion nobody had purchased.

Martin was an adult straight man with a cheerful voice and the confidence of somebody accustomed to explaining what would appeal to everyone. He asked whether the photograph could look a little less like a drag show and more like a coalition.

Velvet folded one arm across the other.

"What do you think a coalition looks like?"

"A broader group."

"You're looking at one."

He said he meant the general public. Rae asked which people in the room had ceased to be members of it when they put their clothes on.

I enjoyed that question so much I nearly repeated it into the microphone. Nia took the microphone off its stand and passed it to Remy before I could turn somebody else's irritation into my own grand moment.

Martin tried to clarify. He wanted the picture to look welcoming. The glitter, the posture, the deliberate styling might appear confrontational to some guests.

Kit glanced at Rae. This time she did not rush to explain Rae's expression for her.

Rae said, "Which posture?"

Martin looked at the camera rather than at her. "I'm not singling anybody out."

"You're already choosing who counts as the public. Tell us who gets left out."

The room became quiet. Owen set his camera on the table.

Martin admitted that he had asked Rae to soften her expression during an earlier test shot. He had described Kit's equally serious face as strong. Hearing the two instructions together embarrassed him more effectively than anything I could have purchased.

Rae did not smile to reward the admission.

"I don't need to perform friendly twice as hard so your brochure can feel relaxed."

Kit looked at her own test image. "And I don't want my picture used as the reasonable version of hers."

June gave a short approving noise from the front row. Then she told both younger women that neither was required to keep a serious expression out of principle if something was funny.

"Nigga, don't let the photographer steal your laugh just because you won't sell it."

Rae laughed at that, which was June's joke earning a response, not Martin's request finally being obeyed.

Owen asked whether everyone wanted a break before the group photograph. Rae said yes. Velvet said she wanted her individual stage pictures first, under the terms already agreed. Kit went to find her glasses. Remy tested the microphone with a joke so bad Martin laughed before remembering he was in trouble.

"You're allowed," Remy told him. "The joke's terrible for everybody."

During the break, Kit sat beside Velvet and asked whether she got tired of having every elaborate outfit treated as a declaration about her entire existence.

Velvet removed one earring. "Sometimes I want it to be a declaration. Sometimes I want you to notice I paid somebody to sew the damn hem."

"How do people know which?"

"They can ask a question smaller than what are you."

Velvet remembered one gay club booking where a man who called her family had then asked her to work for less. Another man at the same club had quietly fixed the payment before the show. She liked remembering both, especially because neither account let anybody use belonging as a discount code.

Kit nodded. She talked about enjoying a good jacket without wanting it interpreted as either a failure to be a woman or a promise to behave like a man. Rae joined them but did not simply echo her. She liked the word stud. It connected to a Black lesbian world she recognized, to people and style and ways of carrying herself that were not available for anybody else's casual relabeling.

"I like what we recognise in each other. I don't want to make your word mine," Kit said.

"Good. I like what we share," Rae said. "I'm still going to tell you when you get me wrong."

June leaned forward. "And leave room for an old Black butch. Some of us were here before your categories got assigned hotel rooms."

Dez touched her sleeve. "You were here before the chairs."

"Still more comfortable than that first jukebox stool."

The room laughed, then returned to the conversation without making either veteran an honorary textbook.

Remy unfastened the small crown from his costume. As King Receipts he could make himself grander, louder, and deliberately ridiculous. As Remy he wanted his date to know he was nervous about the flowers.

"I don't stop being me when the crown comes off," he said. "I just stop charging the room interest."

Velvet snorted. "Keep that one. It almost worked."

Nia asked Rae whether she liked being seen as protective. Rae considered the question.

"Sometimes. When I choose it. I like taking care of people. I also like somebody noticing I'm tired before handing me another box."

Nia set down the box she had been about to offer.

"Oh."

"That one was funny."

They smiled, but the question stayed useful. Caring could be pleasure. It could also become a job people assigned by looking at a body, a jacket, a voice, or the person standing beside it. Rae did not want her tenderness denied. She wanted the right to decide what she did with it.

Kit admitted that she sometimes enjoyed being read as competent before she had earned it. The temptation was especially strong when an event already treated her confidence as less alarming than Rae's. She could not fix that by pretending nobody noticed race, or by claiming Rae's experiences as another version of her own.

"I can stop accepting the comparison as a compliment," she said.

"That's a start," Rae answered. "It doesn't require me to grade the rest of your life."

Owen returned and asked whether they wanted the arrangement kept or changed. He did not call the room boys, girls, masculine, feminine, or brave. He used names. Martin stayed beside him and listened while Mika explained what the picture was for: a record of this evening, not proof that every person outside it would approve.

Mika set one further condition: each person could approve the photograph and caption before the hotel posted either. Nia added that declining the picture would not mean declining the coalition. Martin wrote that down. It was a smaller promise than universal welcome, and one he could actually keep.

I offered to put a political declaration beneath the photograph.

Nia asked which declaration.

"Something powerful."

"Then know what you mean before ordering the lettering."

Shawna rescued me with a more demanding assignment: stand beside her and look as if I wanted to be there.

We made the picture with Rae next to Nia, Kit near Velvet, Remy holding his crown rather than wearing it, and June and Dez comfortably seated. Some people smiled. Some did not. The photographer took more than one image so nobody had to become the single official expression of an identity.

Afterward, Velvet put her earring back on and asked Owen for the stage light she had originally requested. He adjusted it without explaining himself again.

"Nigga," she said to me, "now watch the entrance."

She stepped through the curtain. The room belonged to her for that moment because she knew exactly what she was doing, and because the rest of us finally had the sense to look.

## The Pen Was Tested on Paper That Did Not Bind Anybody

We reached the rehearsal where everything looked ready enough to tempt me into a premature conclusion. The curtain worked. The light worked. Remy's microphone no longer produced a sound like a distressed kitchen appliance.

I picked up the charter.

Nia put a blank sheet beneath my hand.

"Practice paper."

"Nigga, I know what paper is."

"Then you'll appreciate the distinction."

Rae sat at the table and wrote her name. The pen worked, the table stayed still, and the vase remained far enough away to contribute nothing except looking like a vase. Kit sat next, then Velvet, who signed her stage name with an extravagant sweep that cost no one an extra chair.

Remy drew a small crown. Mika sketched a tiny hotel. Tank wrote DINNER and underlined it twice.

June examined both sides of the blank sheet before writing anything. Dez watched her, then turned the sheet over with a look that made fifty-nine years of Blue Comet argument briefly visible in one wrist movement.

"We can use the same side this time," she said.

June laughed. She did not pick up the actual agreement. Neither did Dez. The moment was a possibility, not a settlement I had permission to announce.

Shawna drew a small heart on the practice page and handed me the pen. I started writing an extravagant dedication. She tapped the little space beside her heart.

"Here."

I wrote our initials, which proved sufficient for the task.

Mika gathered the practice sheets and left the real charter untouched in its tray. Nia still wanted to check the final wording. People still had their own conversations to finish. The room could be ready without requiring everybody inside it to move at the same speed.

I asked whether we could at least have a photograph of the successful rehearsal. Velvet said yes, after she adjusted one earring. Remy waited. Kit moved the lamp. For once, the picture happened when the people were ready instead of when I declared the light historically significant.

## The Stage Could Hold the Peace, If We Ever Finished Talking

At the final equipment check, the table stood still. I pressed one corner to confirm this personally, then another because I disliked being excluded from a successful test.

Rae watched me. "You can stop trying to make it interesting."

The curtain opened. Velvet stepped through, made her turn, and reached the microphone with her costume intact. Remy followed at the agreed distance, delivered one deliberately terrible fanfare, and bowed before the joke became an endurance event. Kit found the light flattering enough to defend publicly.

Mika checked the route from the quiet room. June took it at her own pace. Dez walked beside her with the Blue Comet invoice safely inside her bag. They could reach the table without climbing, squeezing past my portrait, or listening to an explanatory recording about why the route was grand.

Mercedes played a few notes. Porsche listened from the seat she had chosen. Tank set down the snack tray where it could be reached, and Rosa immediately proved the placement successful.

"Nigga," I said, "look what we built."

Shawna looked at the room. Then she looked at me.

"Yes. We did."

The word we landed properly that time. It included the hotel workers, the people who measured, the people who asked for a chair, the people who cut a bad idea, and the people whose costume needed more room than my first sketch allowed. It also included me, though not always in the position I had drawn for myself.

I picked up the lever one last time. Remy asked whether I wanted it in the museum or the return box.

"The return box."

Tank put a hand to his chest as if witnessing a miracle. I threatened to order something just to restore his understanding of the world. He handed me a plate before I could act.

The new charter remained unsigned. Its final wording belonged to the next conversations, including matters too personal for my microphone. Nia crossed the room to Rae with no page in her hand. Rae set down the toolkit. Whatever she asked next was quiet enough that neither I nor the ceremony needed to own it.

June and Dez sat beside the finished stage. One remembered the first Blue Comet song; the other remembered the last. Mercedes asked them to hum both. The versions disagreed, but she found a few notes that let them begin together.

I almost announced the second war over. Shawna kissed the beginning of the announcement away.

"Not yet."

"Then what now?"

She took my hand and led me toward the seats. "Let them talk. Sit with me."

The stage was ready. The paper could wait. I sat down before somebody found another useful thing for me to carry, and discovered that this, too, counted as contributing to the peace.

## My Summit Had Two Eyewitnesses and Neither Endorsed Me

By the time we reached the final wording, the casino convention floor contained a working signing table, an actual clear aisle and a portrait of me big enough to possess its own weather. Nigga, peace had acquired infrastructure.

Mika stood beneath the portrait with a tape measure. They said it might have to leave through the loading entrance. I said that was no way to treat the face of reconciliation.

'It's the width of reconciliation,' Mika replied.

Shawna touched my arm. 'Baby, stop negotiating with the tape.'

At the good table, Rae had put a small wedge under the troublesome leg. Nia watched her check it, put the tools away and return to the draft. My wife caught me watching Nia watch Rae.

'Leave it alone,' she whispered. 'I was observing a promising alliance.' 'They can flirt without a ribbon cutting.'

Across the room sat the women whose memories had helped turn my game night into The Second Great Butch vs. Stud War. Auntie June, eighty-two, retired bus driver and proud butch, had commandeered the chair with the best view of the music. Odessa, known as Dez, eighty-four, retired seamstress and equally proud stud, sat beside her holding the disputed jacket.

They agreed the trouble began at the Blue Comet Social Club in 1967. They disagreed about the song, the weather, the jacket's destination and whether June had ever said she was sorry.

'I said it was unfortunate,' June told Nia.

'That the jukebox broke,' Dez said. 'You didn't mean my coat.'

I offered to appoint a historical commission. June looked at me. 'You got biscuits?'

Rosa brought biscuits before I could explain the commission's mandate. Tank followed with tea. My brother had identified which contribution would receive the more favourable account.

The original peace agreement was supposedly unsigned. June said someone lost the pen. Dez said the pen went home in June's pocket. June said a good crossword was not going to complete itself.

Nia asked what they wanted settled tonight. Dez could return June's jacket, then borrow it again by asking. Everybody could choose a jukebox song. The old stories did not have to become identical.

'And nobody makes me play something because they bought it,' Dez added.

'That sentence belongs in there,' Rae said.

I looked toward the portrait. Its expression suggested generosity without limits. Its invoice suggested limits should have arrived considerably earlier.

Velvet Payroll crossed the floor in half her costume, carrying the other half like an expensive weather event. She wanted her show time confirmed. Remy, currently becoming King Receipts, wanted the working microphone and a place for the ridiculous fanfare he had defended through four separate departments.

Kit, a white butch with excellent opinions about her own entrance, wanted to sing under the light she had chosen. Mercedes wanted her arrangement heard. Porsche wanted one photograph everybody actually agreed to stand in. None of these wishes required another summit about what sort of person had permission to want them.

Nia put her name beside both caucuses she belonged to and carried on correcting the last sentence. Rae passed her a cup. The room survived this overlap without installing a second Nia.

I said I was delighted by the complexity of our coalition.

'Nigga, drink your tea,' Velvet told me.

Rae asked Nia whether the pen always made her writing look like that. Nia admitted the pen was innocent. Rae turned the draft sideways, smiling. 'I can learn it.'

Something quiet happened between them. Not mysterious. Two adults taking pleasure in the particular person across the table.

I almost called the photographer.

Shawna closed my hand around my cup instead. 'You can witness something without owning the picture.'

June asked Dez which song she intended to choose. Dez said it would be a surprise. June declared surprises responsible for at least half the original war.

Mika dimmed the portrait's lamp to improve the table light. My enormous forehead disappeared from the ceiling. The actual people became easier to see.

I sat beside my wife, accepted a biscuit and opened the next story.

The room had enough narrators. For a little while, I intended to hear some of them.

## The Dance Was Not a Reward for Being Useful

Nia's invitation reached Rae just as Kit asked whether Rae could fix the little light above the karaoke screen. Rae had spent most of the evening making objects less likely to collapse. She put the note down without reading it and reached for her tools.

Nia covered the tool bag with her hand.

'You can say no,' she said.

Kit looked from one woman to the other. 'I asked. I didn't issue an order.'

'Then let her answer before you tell the technician she's coming.'

The technician stood behind Kit holding a ladder. Nigga, witnesses had developed terrible timing.

I offered to buy another light. All three women ignored me with impressive coordination.

Rae took her hand off the bag. 'I don't want to climb anything. I want to read this note.'

Kit turned to the technician. 'I'm sorry. I assumed.' He nodded and carried the ladder toward the lamp. Kit watched him go. 'We already had this argument over the fees. Apparently I can understand a budget faster than I can stop doing it.'

The less practical problem stayed.

'You could have told me,' Kit said.

'I just did.'

Nia moved her hand away. Rae did not pick up the tools.

Kit was white, butch, wearing a carefully chosen suit and the expression of somebody discovering that a useful intention had arrived badly. Rae was a Black stud with a mechanic's hands and several very specific reasons to dislike being treated as the room's available solution.

I had printed their labels across opposite sides of a banner. It looked impressive from the lift. Up close it had done a remarkably poor job of explaining either woman.

'When I walk into a room like this,' Kit said, 'I already feel as though people are waiting for me to prove I can be useful. I thought we were doing the same thing.'

'We can recognise something without having the same night,' Rae replied.

Kit folded her arms, caught herself and let them drop. 'I know that.'

'You might. You still sent the ladder.'

Velvet sat on the edge of the table. She had heard enough to stop arranging her entrance and start listening.

Kit looked at Rae's tool bag. 'I liked that you seemed certain. You knew what to do with the table. I was still trying to ask for the right light without apologising for having a face.'

'You thought certainty meant I wasn't tired.'

'Maybe.'

Rae looked at the note beneath her hand. 'Sometimes I like fixing things. Sometimes I like being good at something in front of a woman I want. Both can be true, and I can still want the next person to leave the screwdriver alone.'

Nia smiled, but only briefly.

'You don't have to earn this chair,' she said.

Rae turned toward her. 'I know.'

'Do you?'

The room got quiet enough for my portrait's ventilation fan to sound obscene.

I reached for its switch. Shawna pointed to the correct one before I blacked out the entire floor.

Nia waited until the fan stopped. 'I like the way you look at me. I like your terrible opinions about the biscuits. I wanted to flirt with you. Then every time something happened, I became the person who could make your answer sound diplomatic.'

'I didn't ask you to do that,' Rae said.

'No. I did it. I'm stopping.'

She put the marked-up draft on the table. The gesture was small. Rae watched it as though Nia had moved a wall.

'I'm Black, trans, a lesbian, a femme and a lawyer,' Nia said. 'Tonight you have all managed to remember the lawyer whenever a sentence becomes awkward. I would like the woman in the nice dress to get a turn.'

Velvet lifted her glass. 'The dress has been waiting patiently.'

Nia laughed. Rae did not reach for a polished reply.

'I don't want you to translate me,' she said. 'I want you to tell me when I'm being an ass. Preferably before it becomes a programme item.'

'You're being an ass about accepting help.'

'Excellent. Efficient. No billable preamble.'

Kit sat, leaving room between their chairs instead of turning the whole exchange into a panel.

'I don't want the banner to decide what I can ask you,' she said. 'But I can see I've been using same side when I meant please recognise me.'

Rae nodded. 'Ask for that. Don't send equipment.'

June arrived with tea and looked at the banner. 'White butches over here, Black studs over there. Where did you intend to put my Black butch ass?'

I began to explain visual balance.

'Try the chair,' June said, and sat wherever she pleased.

Dez followed. She put the borrowed jacket over June's chair and took the cup June offered her. The banner had lost another jurisdiction.

Kit looked at June. 'I grew up thinking there was one way to look like I belonged. Then I spent years resenting people who looked at ease in it.'

'Who looked at ease?' June asked.

Kit laughed despite herself. 'Fair.'

'I like being butch,' Kit continued. 'I like how my shoulders sit in this jacket. I like a woman calling me handsome without sounding surprised by her own taste. I don't want to speak about all of it as damage.'

'Good,' Rae said. 'Because the jacket looks good. I noticed before we argued.'

Kit looked pleased, then slightly embarrassed by how pleased. Nia told her to enjoy the compliment without preparing a counterstatement.

Rae rubbed one hand over her knee. 'Stud is my word. It doesn't mean I'm volunteering to be a man in somebody else's romance. It doesn't mean I don't want tenderness because I like this shirt.'

Nia touched the cuff, waiting until Rae turned her hand toward hers.

'I like this shirt too,' she said. 'I also like when you stop arranging the space around me long enough to ask where I want to stand.'

'I was trying to make a path.'

'I know. Sometimes I want the path. Sometimes I want your hand. They're different requests.'

I felt Shawna glance at me. Nigga, a lesson had crossed the room without my name appearing anywhere in it.

Remy came over carrying the working microphone. He had missed the start, asked what was happening and accepted Kit's short answer instead of inventing one.

'My gay friends sometimes introduce me as the one who understands women,' he said. 'I'm a man with one particular history. I'm not a customer-service desk for everybody they date.'

Velvet nodded. 'And I put on a queen because I want this room watching the number I rehearsed. That doesn't entitle anybody to invent the rest of my life from the costume.'

'They do enjoy a convenient character,' Kit said.

'So do I,' Velvet replied. 'Mine charges.'

The joke loosened something without ending the conversation. Kit asked Rae whether she wanted another coffee. Rae said water. Kit brought water and did not make the correction into a test of her goodness.

Nia finally picked up the note. 'Now can somebody tell me whether this invitation is legible?'

Rae read it sideways. 'Are you asking me to dance or to inspect a second table?'

'Dance.'

'Then ask.'

'Will you dance with me after the signing?'

'Yes. And if I'm nervous, don't let me pretend I need to check the furniture.'

Nia smiled fully. 'If I'm nervous, don't let me turn it into a contract.'

'You can both be nervous,' Shawna said. 'The floor will cope.'

Rae looked at Nia's hand. 'When we get there, will you hold me first? I keep reaching like I'm supposed to know the whole way.'

'I'd like that,' Nia said. She offered her hand, palm up. Rae took it. Nothing about her shirt, her name or her chosen word needed altering for the gesture to fit.

I offered to have the floor inspected. Shawna put one finger against my lips.

Mercedes asked what song they wanted. They chose together. Kit wanted her own song afterwards; Velvet wanted the time she had booked; Remy wanted his ridiculous fanfare to survive being funny.

Nobody's desire dissolved into the couple's. The room held several wants at once, untidily, without arranging them into opposing armies.

Rae folded the note and kept it. Nia asked why. 'Because you made a bad drawing of a good question,' Rae said.

'That's my handwriting.'

'I know. I'm learning it.'

I looked at the banner again. Its enormous words could still sell a theatrical war. They could not do this part: two women admitting what the pose concealed, another recognising what she had assumed, and June refusing to move to make my categories prettier.

I asked Mika to lower it before the music. Mika asked where to put it.

Shawna pointed at my portrait's transport crate. 'Plenty of room for another oversized explanation.'

Nigga, I held the crate open myself.

## The Final Wording Left My Face Out of It

Nia read the finished wording once, slowly enough for everybody to follow. No heroic music beneath it. Remy had offered, but even he agreed that a fanfare could make a sentence about borrowing coats sound like a siege.

People could choose a game, ask for help, watch, take a break or decline. Sharing a controller required an actual agreement about who did what. The jukebox belonged to everyone's choices. Borrowing the old jacket began with asking the person who currently had it.

My portrait appeared nowhere.

I cleared my throat.

Shawna looked at me. 'You signed that order yourself.'

'I haven't raised the matter.'

'You raised your reimbursement throat.'

Rae laughed. Nia waited until the room settled, then asked whether the wording described what we had actually agreed.

June wanted it clear that she could still say Dez remembered the weather wrong. Dez wanted it clear that she could still point out the jacket's excellent lining.

'You can both keep telling your stories,' Nia said. 'This settles tonight's arrangements.'

They approved. The old war did not need a winner to stop acquiring new invoices.

Velvet checked that her paid performance stayed paid regardless of whether everybody watched. Remy checked his cue. Kit asked for the lamp to remain where she could read the song list. Mika checked the clock and looked briefly overcome by the astonishing possibility that the gala might begin.

Rosa brought the last tray past the table without catching her sleeve. Rae's repaired leg stayed steady. Tank sat beside her and declared the engineering department a success.

Nia put down the pen. Rae took her hand under the edge of the table. I saw their shoulders relax at the same time.

'Still after the signatures?' Rae asked.

'Still,' Nia said.

I wanted to tell them that a great romance deserved an audience. Then I remembered several great romantic moments in my own marriage had occurred specifically because the audience left.

Shawna caught my eye. The woman could follow a terrible idea across my face before I found words expensive enough to decorate it.

'Good choice, baby,' she said.

'You don't know what I chose.'

'I know what you didn't say.'

The clean draft went into its folder. June and Dez rose slowly, helping each other without deciding which assistance counted toward the coat account. They would return for the signing after the last shared-play trial.

Mercedes touched the first chord of the chosen dance song. Rae looked toward the floor; Nia watched Rae.

Mika asked whether my portrait's lamp could stay off for the rest of the evening.

I looked at the faces already lit around the table.

'Yeah,' I said. 'Leave it.'

Nigga, the final wording was agreed. Nobody had surrendered a name, a story or the right to go home. I had surrendered one unnecessary spotlight, which felt like enough personal history for tonight.
