## The Rehearsal Had Two Controllers and One Unnecessary Throne

I placed two controllers on a velvet cushion beneath the portrait. It was meant to suggest equality. Tank looked at the cushion, then at the only chair facing the screen.

'Where's the other person sit?'

Nigga, equality had arrived ahead of the furniture.

Rae pulled up a second chair. Nia moved the cushion so both controllers could reach their cables. My wife sat in the chair I had reserved for the host and asked whether I planned to stand there explaining the arrangement all night.

'I'm establishing the mood.'

'You've established a queue.'

The final wording waited in its folder. The signing table stood level, the light reached the page and Mika had timed the walk from the buffet without including any pause for my autobiography. We were going to try sharing actual controls before celebrating an agreement about sharing a room.

Dez arrived wearing the disputed jacket. Auntie June followed carrying its empty hanger.

'Evidence,' June told me.

Dez said a hanger could not prove the weather in 1967. June said she had brought it to hang the coat, which was a far more devastating reply than any courtroom flourish I could have supplied.

Both veterans still claimed the other had never signed the old Blue Comet agreement. This one had acquired enough working pens to alarm a stationery wholesaler. I had bought the gold one. Nia preferred the plain black one because it actually wrote.

Rae tested both. 'Yours writes too,' she told Nia. 'Just not in a recognised direction.'

Nia smiled. 'You understood the invitation.'

'Eventually.'

They would dance after the signing. Their only unresolved question was whether Rae could persuade Nia that being good at a contract did not require counting every step before the music began.

Kit had her karaoke song ready and her reading glasses attached to a cord. Remy admired the practical innovation, then discovered his crown prevented him from putting on his headphones.

Velvet Payroll removed the crown, set it on the table and told him to preserve his head for the performance. She had been paid, her shoes were fastened and her stage time existed on an actual clock. A powerful woman with excellent grounds for happiness.

Mercedes checked the music. Porsche checked that the photographer understood which pictures people wanted. Nobody needed another staged candid in which Rae pretended not to notice a lens six inches from her coffee.

Dre brought the blue controller and a casserole. He was a Crip with a hot dish, not an available metaphor for my summit title. He wanted a clear space to set the food and the particular colour of plastic he had chosen.

I offered the gold controller. 'Nigga, you keep the expensive-looking problem,' he said.

Darnell appeared behind him with a little case and an offer to sponsor fireworks. Velvet asked whether the sponsorship involved money or cocaine. He said relationships. She told him her actual relationships had already paid for the show.

He tried describing a yacht. The host opened the lift before the description acquired a second deck. Darnell went to find a different audience. Dre stayed to ask Rosa whether the casserole needed warming.

Mika suggested using the model hotel to rehearse the procession. I liked the idea until they assigned my paper figure to hold the door.

'I have a speaking role.'

'You have a useful arm,' Rae said.

Shawna kissed that arm through my sleeve. Suddenly the assignment developed possibilities.

Some games would give two people separate characters. Some would divide their information. Some would give one person a smaller helping role. Others could simply be enjoyed together with one person operating the controls.

June said she might watch. Dez said she might try. Neither statement triggered an emergency meeting.

I looked up at the portrait, whose enormous expression appeared to endorse every arrangement. That was generous of it, considering the evening had still authorised none of its cost.

Then Rae handed Nia a controller and asked which role she wanted. A normal question, asked without a trumpet.

I sat beside Shawna, took the other available chair properly and waited to hear the answer.

The Second Great Butch vs. Stud War had reached the dangerous stage where people might enjoy themselves enough to forget who was supposed to receive credit.

## Peace Could Not Be Purchased with My Portrait Budget

The disagreement started with a line on the hotel's final service sheet: HOST TO DETERMINE PARTICIPANT SUITABILITY. I thought it meant deciding who could fit into Remy's spare crown.

Nia read it again. Rae put down her water.

'Suitable for what?' Rae asked.

The floor manager said it was standard wording. Nigga, people kept presenting standard as though it meant nobody had chosen it.

Kit asked whether it gave the door staff discretion to stop a guest who looked difficult. The manager said they would use judgment.

'Whose?' June asked.

I began saying the hotel was very welcoming. Shawna touched my sleeve. 'Let them answer.'

The manager explained that the host could approve the guest list. I was the host. Suddenly the expensive room had handed me a power I had been enjoying without examining its edges.

Rae said a security guard had asked her twice that afternoon whether she was working here. The second time, she was carrying her own coffee. Kit had walked beside her with a lighting cable and received a welcome.

'I told him she was with us,' Kit said.

Rae looked at her. 'I was already with myself.'

Kit nodded, embarrassed. 'I know. That's what came out.'

'It helped him stop asking. It also made you the person who could confirm I belonged.'

The manager said the guard was only checking. Velvet asked why checking had required the same person twice.

I recognised the expression on the manager's face. It was the one I used when I wanted a complaint to become a misunderstanding before anybody priced the remedy.

Nia did not translate Rae's sentence into nicer language. She asked the manager to answer it.

He could not explain the difference in treatment. He said he would speak to the guard.

Rae asked what would happen if it happened again while everybody was busy watching the stage. The manager gave his own name and said he would stay on the floor. Mika wrote down the number he supplied and checked that the phone rang.

A small test. No fanfare. A real person expected to answer.

Kit said she would correct her own introduction if it happened again. 'I don't need to tell him you're with me. I need to tell him he's already been answered.'

'And when I'm not standing there,' Rae said.

'Yes.'

The manager took the sheet away to replace the vague line. I watched him go, wondering why it had seemed so harmless until somebody described being on its receiving end.

June set her cup down. 'Your invitation put us on opposite sides before we got through the door. Then your hotel decided who looked like staff.'

I said the war title was a joke.

'I laughed,' she replied. 'I'm still asking you something.'

That stopped me more effectively than anger would have. I knew how to posture against an accusation. I had less practice staying still inside a question asked by someone who did not need to dislike me.

Rae touched the edge of the table she had repaired. 'I like making things work. I don't want that to become the price of being the kind of woman I am in this room.'

Kit said she recognised the temptation to earn welcome through competence. Then she stopped herself.

'That's my experience,' she said. 'It doesn't finish yours.'

Rae nodded. The distinction did not turn either of them into an enemy.

June tapped the portrait crate, where my folded war banner now lived. 'And I remain a Black butch whether your campaign knows where to put me or not. Don't use me as the exception that excuses the arrangement.'

'I won't,' I said.

She waited. I checked the entrance myself. The new signs named the rooms and where to ask for help. The banner stayed in its crate. The main title could remain the title of our absurd story without becoming sorting instructions for arriving guests.

Dez watched me straighten a sign. 'Careful with the corner. That's how jackets start wars.'

The laugh helped. It did not return the conversation to where it had been.

Mika brought the remaining staff costs. The performers had been paid, but the technicians' booked finish time came before the extra photographs I had requested. Someone would be packing down while I pretended the room existed indefinitely.

I offered the portrait's lighting budget.

'That money is already spent,' Nia said.

'A symbolic transfer.'

'The technician takes actual money,' Velvet replied.

Remy asked to cut his second entrance so the work could end on time. Velvet refused to solve my extension by making his performance smaller. Kit offered to shorten her own song, then admitted she did not really want to.

Nobody applauded her sacrifice. She looked relieved.

Rosa said the people clearing plates also had homes to reach. Tank moved the empty trays onto the trolley instead of describing his solidarity with the catering profession.

I asked the manager for the real cost of the time I had added. He returned with a number. It was less than the frame around my face.

Nigga, the comparison did something unpleasant to my priorities.

I paid the extension. We also ended the extra photo session early. Money bought the agreed work; it did not make staying late everyone's natural obligation.

Nia put the corrected sheet beside the game-night charter. 'These are arrangements for tonight. They don't buy forgiveness, desire or a story in which everybody now understands everybody.'

Mika put the remaining voluntary contributions on the table. The money had been collected for microphones and getting people home. I suggested applying it to the hotel's final total. Velvet asked which contributors had agreed to buy my decorations.

Kit pushed the envelope back toward Mika. 'I put in what I could. That doesn't buy me a better chair, and it doesn't become somebody else's portrait because the cheque was small.'

Rae proposed checking each remaining expense with Kit against the stated purposes. Mika would keep the record visible to contributors. Anything left would go back by the arrangement they had actually accepted. No surprise donation to my face.

I accepted that. The envelope stayed on their side of the table. Nigga, shared money had developed a location outside my pocket.

'Do they buy my dance?' I asked Shawna, attempting a recovery.

'No. I happen to want you. Don't make it accounting.'

Rae smiled at Nia. Nia smiled back, then turned toward the room. 'I also don't want our dance used as proof that the summit worked. I asked a woman I like to dance. That gets to be smaller than your campaign.'

I nodded. Porsche removed the planned photograph from the list without asking Nia to defend it.

Porsche asked what should happen if a recording continued after somebody said stop. Rae wanted it stopped, not debated over her head. Kit wanted a named person to take the request so the person objecting did not have to chase the whole room.

Mika took that job for the event. The photographer agreed to check a shot before using it and to set disputed material aside. If the plan broke, the recording would pause while the people involved decided the next step. An apology would not substitute for stopping the camera.

Nia approved the arrangement and declined the job of supervising it. She had a dance to attend. Porsche lowered her phone to show she had heard.

Remy sat on the arm of a chair. 'When people argue about whether men belong in a room, I hear the word differently from the way I did before transition. I still want friendships with women. I don't want my being a man treated as either a betrayal or a useful exception.'

June asked what he wanted tonight.

'My name used correctly. My number heard. My terrible fanfare tolerated once.'

'Once is a strong negotiating position,' Dez said.

Velvet flicked his crown with one finger. 'He is still responsible for the pun. Coalition will not save him.'

I liked that. Responsibility could remain particular. Nobody had to defend an entire category before admitting one man's joke was bad.

Kit asked whether our agreement should include never offending each other. Rae said no. She wanted people to stop, listen and repair what they could when they did. She did not promise to become instantly comfortable because the apology sounded polished.

Kit accepted that without asking how long Rae's patience would last.

The corrected service sheet returned. Nia read it; Mika checked the contact details; Rae said it answered the practical question she had asked. June asked whether everybody could still decline a game without being asked to explain their mood.

That line was already there. We kept it.

Dez reached for the jacket on her chair. 'And can we finally settle the sleeve business?'

Dez said she would return the coat when they signed. Could she then borrow it for the walk downstairs? June said yes.

Fifty-nine years of comedy briefly reduced itself to a question that could have been asked over a jukebox. Neither woman looked diminished by the answer.

I looked at the portrait crate. No communal payment, no title granting me the last word, no proof that I had become a better man merely because the floor was expensive.

Shawna took my hand anyway.

'You staying?' I asked.

'For the signing. For the dance. For you, if you stop trying to invoice the feeling.'

I kissed her hand, paid the remaining real workers and helped Mika clear the path to the table.

Peace was not everybody agreeing that I meant well.

Tonight, it was a door that stayed open, a number somebody would answer, work somebody would pay for, and enough room for two women to choose a song without becoming my evidence.

## P238 - Dinkum

### In one sentence

Build a town and explore an Australian-inspired landscape with friends, choosing whether default survival or the separate Creative Mode better suits the appeal of making a place.

### What you do

Gather resources, farm, build and meet residents, or inspect Creative Mode before deciding which shared town activities to pursue.

### How you play

Movement + camera | Action continues while you think | Native co-op in this edition

### Main catch

Default play includes wildlife and combat; camera comfort, visitor permissions and some host-only town tasks still need checking.

### Edition considered

PC release; current version status must be checked

### Editorial starting point

P238  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Explore, gather, farm and build a settlement in an Australian-inspired landscape, meeting residents and inviting friends online. The full PC release combines town creation with survival and also includes a separate Creative Mode, offering a different focus for building.

### The full catch

Default play includes wild animals, tools, combat, gathering, crafting and a three-dimensional view. Creative Mode changes building options, not the need to check camera comfort. Official launch notes leave some town quests to the host. Record the installed version rather than relying on old Early Access advice.

### Try this first

Try walking, looking around and one modest town task before entering dangerous terrain. Inspect Creative Mode if building is the attraction, then check the chosen multiplayer permissions. Ask whether both players enjoy their available tasks rather than assigning one all the work.

### Aiden at the summit

The Town Host Needed Permission Too

Dinkum's shared town plans made Mika ask who would control the summit's remaining decorations after tonight. I answered as though ownership were an atmospheric quality surrounding my jacket.

Rae asked who had actually built the useful pieces. Mika raised a hand. Kit raised one. Remy lifted the repaired arch. Velvet pointed at the light she had helped position.

Nia wrote that people could take their own contributions home, borrow by asking and leave unwanted ornaments for the person who bought them.

Everybody looked at me. Nigga, the portrait had become an unusually specific weather front.

The game's modes and visitor permissions needed checking before promising equal freedom. Our room needed the same ordinary clarity about whose thing was whose.

June returned the old jacket to Dez. Dez immediately offered it back for the walk to the car. This time June asked how long.

Dez returned the old jacket to June. Then Dez asked to borrow it for the walk to the car. June asked how long.

'Until you're cold,' Dez said.

### Aiden’s verdict

Build the town if the chosen mode and visitor roles suit. Our borrowing agreement has successfully returned one jacket and left the portrait with its extensively documented purchaser.

### Evidence desk

Matched PC Steam description supports Australian-inspired survival, farming and online cooperation. Official launch announcements explicitly confirm the April 23, 2025 UTC exit from Early Access, Creative Mode and revised multiplayer permissions. Some town/building quests remain host-only in those launch notes. Current build behavior still needs checking; observed September 20, 2026.

## P239 - Farm Together

### In one sentence

Grow and decorate a shared farm that keeps moving while you are offline, making return visits part of the pleasure without requiring continuous attendance from players.

### What you do

Plant and tend crops, care for animals, arrange the farm and set permissions for friends helping with the ongoing work.

### How you play

Movement + camera | Some real-time demands | Native co-op in this edition

### Main catch

Repeated tending and expansion can become a workload; check camera controls, menus and permissions, and remember this is the first game.

### Edition considered

PC first game

### Editorial starting point

P239  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Grow crops, keep animals, decorate a farm and invite other players to cultivate it together. The first Farm Together explicitly lets time progress while you are offline, creating a place that can be revisited rather than requiring continuous attendance.

### The full catch

Repeated tending, expansion, currencies, waiting and item menus can become a workload. Movement and camera handling need a direct check. Online farm permissions matter when sharing; the source does not establish every activity as untimed or hold-free. This card covers the first game, not its sequel.

### Try this first

Plant or tend one small area and inspect how a friend joins and what they may change. Try camera movement and a basic interaction. Decide whether returning to growing things feels pleasant without agreeing to an attendance schedule.

### Aiden at the summit

The Farm Kept Growing While the Pen Went Around

Farm Together's continuing little tasks made Tank wonder whether a place could carry on without its host supervising every minute. Rae looked at me. Nia looked at me. Shawna spared a glance.

I said I was sensing an unrelated agenda.

Rosa liked the idea of returning to a shared farm for a modest job. She also liked the right to leave it alone when dinner, sleep or other people sounded better.

June passed the signed page to Dez. Dez read the jukebox sentence once more, smiled and added her name. Nia signed beneath the agreed final wording with her magnificent, terrible handwriting.

Rae recognised it anyway.

The game's persistent work could become pleasant or burdensome depending on what people wanted. Our charter settled that nobody owed a game attendance simply because someone else loved it.

I signed last and discovered the portrait line had not secretly improved.

Shawna kissed my cheek. 'Congratulations, baby. Peace is official.'

'And expensive.' 'That part was official when you ordered the frame.'

### Aiden’s verdict

Return to the shared farm if its ongoing tasks remain pleasant. The coalition is signed, participation stays voluntary, and the portrait's continuing existence does not create collective financial responsibility.

### Evidence desk

Manually verified Steam app 673950 is the first Farm Together, published by Milkstone Studios. Product description explicitly supports shared farming, permissions and time advancing offline. These claims are not imported from Farm Together 2; exact control comfort remains untested.

## P240 - Staxel

### In one sentence

Restore a farm and shape a blocky village with friends online, sharing one place or becoming neighbours while building projects give the world personal character.

Move around the world, place building materials, grow crops and help villagers, coordinating a small farm or construction project with friends.

### How you play

Movement + camera | Some real-time demands | Native co-op in this edition

### Main catch

First-person camera movement, crafting and precise block placement add demands; establish the session setup and check sustained inputs before building.

### Edition considered

PC release

### Editorial starting point

P240  /  READ THE CATCH FIRST

### Why it might click

Restore a farm, meet villagers and alter a voxel world through building and cultivation. The PC game explicitly supports online cooperation, allowing friends to share a farm or become neighbours while making their own projects.

### The full catch

First-person movement, camera steering, selecting materials, crafting and placing blocks can create substantial coordination and menu demands. Farming tasks add routine work. The publisher's creative premise does not certify no holds, no timed activities or a frictionless multiplayer setup.

### Try this first

Try looking around, moving through a doorway and placing or interacting with a simple object. If sharing online, establish who owns the session and how both people join. Choose one small project only after the controls feel worth using.

### Aiden at the summit

The Village Had Enough Room for a Dance

Staxel's shared village made Mika place the last two figures inside the miniature hotel. Rae and Nia stood on its little dance floor. My figure remained near the loading dock.

'A strong logistical role,' I said. 'A safe distance from the music controls,' Kit replied.

The signed agreement lay beneath the lamp. June and Dez had chosen different songs. Both selections would play. June's jacket waited over Dez's arm, borrowed again by asking.

The game's building and first-person controls still needed an actual trial. Our constructed room had already passed a simpler test: people could see, sit, leave and find each other.

Mercedes began the chosen music. Nia held out her hand to Rae. Rae took it without requesting another furniture inspection.

I offered Shawna my own hand. 'No introduction?' she asked. 'I'm trying a local custom.'

She came close. Velvet laughed beside the stage, Remy finally played the right fanfare, and nobody looked toward my portrait for permission.

Nigga, the place had become ours without becoming mine.

### Aiden’s verdict

Make a shared place if its camera and building demands suit. Our finished room offers a dance, an open door and absolutely no reimbursement for the face above it.

### Evidence desk

## Everybody Chose a Song; Nobody Bought My Face

The signatures were real. June wrote slowly, Dez added hers with a seamstress's steady care, and Nia's name crossed the line like an adventurous bird. Rae recognised it and signed beside it. The others followed in an order nobody would need to defend for sixty years.

Dez unfolded the old rental invoice while Nia checked the new names. June pointed at her own 1967 signature. Dez turned the paper over. Hers was on the back.

Both women stared. 'You signed the wrong side,' June said. 'You read the wrong side,' Dez replied. Nigga, I had hired a convention floor to resolve a failure to turn over one sheet.

I signed last. The portrait still received no reimbursement.

'Perhaps a commemorative allowance,' I murmured.

Shawna took the pen from my hand. 'Perhaps enjoy your wife.'

Nigga, finally a motion I could support without amendment.

The agreement protected an ordinary evening. Choose a game, ask for help, watch or decline. Stop when you want. Share the actual controls by agreement. Let different interests occupy the same room without drafting a winner.

Dez returned the jacket to June, then asked to borrow it for the walk downstairs. June said yes, provided it came back before another jukebox became obsolete.

'You make me sound unreliable,' Dez said.

'Only with sleeves,' June replied.

They laughed. The Blue Comet war ended without anyone fixing the weather in the official account.

June's chosen jukebox song played first. Dez tapped the table, pretending she had not liked it since 1967. Her own choice followed, and June sang the chorus incorrectly with magnificent commitment.

Then Mercedes began the song Rae and Nia had chosen.

Nia put her pen down and held out her hand. Rae took it and stood. No further invitation. No scheduling language. They walked onto the floor as two women who had spent the evening finding each other interesting and now wanted to be close.

Nia counted one step, caught Rae smiling and stopped counting aloud. Rae laughed softly. Nia drew a little nearer. Their first turn was imperfect and entirely theirs.

I signalled the photographer out of habit. Porsche touched his arm before he moved. Rae glanced over, shook her head once, and the camera stayed down.

Shawna took both my hands. 'Your turn.'

'For the photograph?'

'For me, nigga.'

I followed her onto the floor. The giant portrait watched from above, useful at last because it could not interrupt.

Velvet finished her number to the applause it deserved. Remy's fanfare arrived at the right moment and still contained the terrible pun. Kit sang. Rosa leaned against Tank; Dre collected the casserole dish only after checking nobody wanted more.

Mika placed the model hotel beside the signed agreement. Its little door remained open.

Later, Dez draped half the borrowed jacket across June's shoulders while they waited for the lift. June pretended the division needed measuring. Dez pulled her closer and said the seam allowance was generous.

The hotel manager handed me the portrait transport charge.

I looked at Shawna. She looked back with no intention of rescuing my budget and every intention of staying beside me.

I paid it.

Then I folded the receipt, put it in my own pocket and returned to the woman holding out her hand. Peace had its own music. For once, I did not need to introduce the singer.

## The Department of Lesbian Lore Has Seized the Microphone

Aiden requested the entire history of lesbians, preferably in a font that made him look responsible. The archive declined the second condition. What follows is a substantial, selective field guide through several histories of desire, community, conflict and organizing. Its dates orient the reader; they do not rank cultures by how far they have progressed.

There is no single family tree that begins in Greece, passes through white Europe and ends by admitting everybody else. Nor can one white-butch/Black-stud rivalry explain the racial boundaries of lesbian life. Read the locally named people, organizations and records here as distinct histories that sometimes meet, rather than stages of one universal development.

Every dossier separates the historical account, a question for interpretation, the limits of the evidence, and a completely fictional summit scene. A source record may be a manifesto, an organizational self-history, an interview, an abstract or a curator’s description. Those are different forms of evidence. An archive finding aid does not mean its whole collection was read.

Pleasure belongs in the history alongside organizing and exclusion. Sexual roles, gender presentation, erotic preference and identity can connect without being interchangeable. This guide discusses desire and sexual politics without converting anyone’s body or boundaries into a spectacle. Aiden supplies enough spectacle already. The fictional 1967 Blue Comet war remains entirely outside the factual timeline.

## Sappho did not leave a membership spreadsheet

### Place and period

Archaic Greek poetry and its later reception

Sappho’s poetry and its reception offer a starting point for a history of women’s desire, not the first box in a universal identity chart. The British Library’s manuscript account distinguishes the surviving fragments from later stories about the poet. Some poems concern love for women; later writers interpreted, celebrated and moralized her life in conflicting ways. Modern sapphic language draws on that legacy, but a contemporary identity vocabulary cannot simply be pasted onto an ancient social world.

The archive itself is part of the story. The Library discusses the loss, copying and difficult language of the poems, and challenges the easy tale that a single coordinated campaign of suppression explains everything missing. A fragment’s survival and a later biographer’s claim are different kinds of evidence. Our editorial inference: wanting an ancestor is understandable; inventing certainty about that ancestor makes the history smaller, not more intimate.

### The question underneath

What do we actually know, and what have later readers wanted an ancestor to prove?

### Evidence limit

Sappho is not made the origin of every culture’s same-sex desire.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

I unveiled the Lesbian Family Tree. It was gold, six feet tall and, because the contractor had misunderstood branching, faintly on fire.

Kit asked where I had put uncertainty. I showed her the cloakroom. June asked where I had put everybody who had never written anything down. I showed her an empty branch.

'Nigga,' Tank said, 'you bought a tree and still managed to lose the forest.'

Mika unplugged it. The historical record immediately became easier to breathe near.

### Read scope

Peter Toth, British Library — The Mystery of Sappho. Curatorial manuscript essay read; no independent Greek translation or complete corpus study.

### Source

## Anne Lister: a lover, a diarist, and a landowner

### Place and period

Yorkshire, 1791–1840

Anne Lister left an unusually extensive record of a woman’s relationships with women alongside business, travel and everyday life. Calderdale Museums describes twenty-six diary volumes, substantial coded passages, estate management and her partnership with Ann Walker. Walker moved to Shibden in 1834. Their relationship was embedded in property, family and the possibilities available to two women with resources; those material conditions belong beside the romance.

That is a reason to resist turning Lister into a generic representative of every woman who desired women in nineteenth-century Britain. A surviving house, a large written record and the ability to travel give this life a particular visibility. The museum documents subsequent preservation and transcription work as well. Editorially, the important contrast is between a detailed individual archive and the lives a comparable archive cannot recover. Recognition need not require calling someone the first, the only, or an uncomplicated political model.

### The question underneath

Whose independence also depended on property, and whose records survived?

### Evidence limit

A partnership ceremony is not presented here as a modern legal marriage.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

I announced that a private archive deserved a private wing. Shawna asked whether I had kept last month’s electricity bill.

'That is contemporary history.'

'It is a final notice.'

Rae studied my model of the wing. 'Does the reading room need a champagne lift?'

I explained access. Nia explained access back to me, more accurately and with substantially fewer moving parts.

### Read scope

Calderdale Museums — Anne Lister. Museum account and description of diary preservation read; full diaries not read.

### Source

https://museums.calderdale.gov.uk/explore/famous-figures/anne-lister

## Mabel Hampton: parties, clothes and remembered words

### Place and period

1920s–1930s, recalled decades later

In interviews with Joan Nestle, Mabel Hampton remembered women gathering near her Harlem home for food, dancing and companionship. She described mostly Black company, while also remembering white friends from Greenwich Village. These recollections preserve a social world with interracial connections without implying that the wider city offered equal welcome. Clothing also depended on movement through public space: Hampton distinguished arriving by car from walking outside in trousers.

Hampton recalled several words used around women who loved women, including butch and sometimes stud. Her testimony records remembered usage, not a single origin or timeless definition for either term. She also described paid sewing and stage work and a lasting relationship with Lillian Foster. The resulting history includes attraction and pleasure alongside the practical arrangements that let people meet, earn money and travel together.

### The question underneath

How does the route to a gathering shape who can dress freely once inside?

### Evidence limit

Later-life memory contains uncertain dates; one person's vocabulary cannot establish universal historical usage.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

I announced that everyone could arrive in whatever made them feel magnificent. June asked why my magnificent complimentary shuttle stopped three blocks away.

'The car photographs better beside the fountain.'

She looked at me for long enough to age the upholstery. Mika redirected the driver. June held the door while Dez climbed in wearing the disputed jacket.

'There,' June said. 'Now the freedom has transport.'

I went to tell the photographer about the fountain's unexpected independence.

### Read scope

Making Gay History: Mabel Hampton (authorized oral-history excerpts, 2026). Read episode notes and the complete edited interview transcript; audio was not auditioned.

### Source

https://makinggayhistory.org/podcast/mabel-hampton/

## Gladys Bentley: performance, desire and the price of public visibility

### Place and period

1920s–1950s

In Harlem, Gladys Bentley earned her living as a blues singer and pianist through parties and nightclub appearances. Suits, a top hat and flirtation with women became elements of her public performance. The American Masters documentary places that career within entertainment opportunities for Black women, while also describing criticism from people concerned with respectable public images of Black life. Celebrity and sexual visibility could coexist with constraint.

Bentley later worked in Los Angeles and altered her public presentation. An early-1950s magazine account presented claims about heterosexual marriage and hormonal treatment; those claims do not settle her private experience. The documentary interprets this turn against repression and employment pressures. Her history therefore invites attention to who controlled a performer's livelihood and reputation, without making stage clothing a reliable certificate of either sexual orientation or a modern gender identity.

### The question underneath

Who gets to read an entertainer's clothes as freedom while ignoring the conditions of her employment?

### Evidence limit

Documentary interpretation and Bentley's public claims are distinguished from independently established private experience.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

The costume consultant looked at Rae's shirt and began explaining Rae to Rae. It took him forty seconds to misplace an entire person.

'The shirt has a label,' she said. 'Try reading that one.'

He identified the washing temperature correctly. Velvet applauded once. Remy gave him a laundry bag instead of a microphone.

I asked whether the consultation was refundable. Nia said that depended on what I had paid him to know. Nigga, the invoice was suddenly very difficult to defend.

### Read scope

American Masters: Gladys Bentley: Gender-Bending Performer and Musician (PBS, 2020). Read the complete online documentary transcript; did not watch the video.

## A novel reaches the prosecutor’s desk

### Place and period

Britain, 1928

The National Archives preserves an August 1928 communication about Radclyffe Hall’s The Well of Loneliness. Its public description identifies a letter concerning possible prosecution for obscene libel; a Home Secretary’s note threatened prosecution if the publisher did not withdraw the book. The accompanying transcript excerpt notes favorable literary reviews. The document makes a specific conflict visible: literary recognition did not prevent the state from treating a representation of lesbian life as a problem to suppress.

This is a record of official scrutiny, not a complete account of Hall, her politics, the novel’s readers or the eventual litigation. It also asks us to separate a work’s historical importance from agreement with every idea inside it. A book can provide recognition and still use concepts its later readers dispute. That last distinction is our reading question, rather than a claim that one prosecution document can summarize lesbian literature.

### The question underneath

Who gets to decide whether depicting desire is itself indecent?

### Evidence limit

The legal claim is limited to the dated document, not current law or a full trial history.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

I appointed myself Head of Dangerous Literature and confiscated the karaoke binder.

Kit waited until I reached the third power ballad. 'What is the alleged danger?'

'Your intention to perform all of these.'

Velvet took the binder back. 'That is a scheduling dispute, sweetheart.'

For a man with a new sash, I was learning a discouraging number of limits to jurisdiction.

### Read scope

The National Archives — Well of loneliness, DPP 1/88. Archive description and indexed transcript excerpt read; direct page returned 403; no complete trial-file inspection.

### Source

## Ruth Ellis and Babe Franklin: a home with room to dance

### Place and period

1940s–1960s

Ruth Ellis and Ceciline 'Babe' Franklin made their Detroit home a gathering place for Black gay and lesbian people who encountered discrimination in bars. Known as the Gay Spot, it offered conversation, laughter and dancing across several decades. The Bentley Historical Library's account connects that hospitality with the couple's daily life, rather than presenting community as something created only by a formal organization or a public demonstration.

Ellis operated a printing business and darkroom from the same home, producing materials for local churches and small businesses. Work, partnership and social space were physically intertwined. Reading the house as community infrastructure is an interpretation grounded in those arrangements: people needed somewhere to gather, and someone had to sustain it. This was a household offering an alternative to commercial nightlife, not evidence that all Detroit venues shared the same exclusions or practices.

### The question underneath

Whose work makes a welcoming room possible when a commercial venue closes its doors?

### Evidence limit

The archival feature synthesizes earlier accounts; underlying collection boxes and the documentary were not examined.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

I declared the room a historic community space. Rosa asked me to carry the folding chairs upstairs.

'Surely there is a ceremonial role.'

She handed me two chairs. 'Both hands.'

By the third trip I understood why history required refreshments. Shawna met me with water and a kiss on the cheek. I tried to turn toward the photographer without spilling either.

'Just enjoy being useful,' she said.

Nigga, it was more exhausting than being admired and significantly better received.

### Read scope

Katie Vloet, Living with Pride (Bentley Historical Library, Fall 2018). Read the library feature, especially The Gay Spot section and its source list.

### Source

https://bentley.umich.edu/about/collections-magazine/fall-2018/living-with-pride/

## The founders the simplified story leaves out

### Place and period

San Francisco, 1955–1956

The Library of Congress’s Daughters of Bilitis guide identifies Filipina Rosalie ‘Rose’ Bamberger as the person who proposed a private lesbian social club. Four couples met in 1955. Rose and her partner Rosemary Sliepen worked in brush manufacturing; the guide also identifies a founding participant known as Mary as Chicana. Del Martin and Phyllis Lyon became prominent figures, but prominence should not erase the other founders.

The organization’s move toward public advocacy created disagreement over exposure and risk. The guide reports that working-class founders were uncomfortable with that direction. The Ladder began in 1956 and built a nationally distributed lesbian readership. This history complicates a simple story of a white middle-class movement later discovering diversity. It also complicates the idea that private social life and public activism were identical needs. Our interpretive question is material: who could afford visibility, and who stood to lose work, privacy or a place to gather?

### The question underneath

When does being visible help, and who bears the cost of becoming visible?

### Evidence limit

Unequal public recognition does not mean lesser participation.

## A manifesto argues that desire is political

### Place and period

Radicalesbians, 1970

The Woman-Identified Woman is an argument by Radicalesbians, not a neutral dictionary entry. The 1970 manifesto treats the threat of being called a lesbian as a means of policing women, including women in liberation movements. It asks women to put their relationships with one another at the center of political life. Its ambitions exceed securing tolerance for a private sexual minority.

Reading it historically also means noticing its sweeping claims about women, men, social roles and sexuality. An influential intervention need not supply the language every later lesbian must accept. We can ask what becomes possible when people refuse shame and what becomes obscured when a shared political category seems to speak for everyone. That question opens room for the racial, class and gender disagreements elsewhere in this field guide. Those are comparisons we invite readers to make; the manifesto itself does not resolve them for us.

### The question underneath

What changes when a private stigma becomes a collective political name?

### Evidence limit

Historical political argument; its generalizations are not adopted as biological or universal facts.

## Salsa Soul Sisters: making a community when the bars excluded you

### Place and period

Founded 1974; subsequent organizing

Salsa Soul Sisters formed in New York in 1974 as a community for lesbians of color. The American LGBTQ+ Museum describes racist bar practices that restricted entry or treated women of color differently once inside. Shared sexuality did not guarantee shared access. Organizing a separate space could therefore answer a concrete exclusion, while allowing members to define cultural and practical priorities themselves.

The group's activities connected poetry, music and dance with information about health and support for women entering jobs outside conventional expectations. Children and family life also belonged within that community. Archival descriptions record publications, retreats, events and meeting materials. Together these sources suggest an organization sustained through repeated work, rather than a single heroic founding moment. Its example complicates a simple opposition between social pleasure and politics: building a place to meet could involve both.

### The question underneath

When does creating a separate room expand participation rather than abandon coalition?

### Evidence limit

Accounts describe particular exclusions and organizational experiences, not every lesbian bar or every member's perspective.

## The archive is also an argument about who matters

### Place and period

Lesbian Herstory Archives, 1970s onward

The Lesbian Herstory Archives describes its origins in groups that formed through the Gay Academic Union during the 1970s. Its mission is to preserve records of lesbian lives and make them available to future generations. The archive’s own digital-resource descriptions name photographs, periodicals, organizational and personal records, shirts, buttons and newsletters. Ordinary possessions and community-made media are evidence, not merely decoration around famous lives.

The 1978 newsletter’s statement of purpose makes the collecting ambition explicit: experiences omitted by dominant historical accounts should be recorded and preserved. Reading this alongside elite diaries changes the question from ‘Who was exceptional enough to remember?’ to ‘What work lets ordinary lives remain knowable?’ This is our interpretive comparison. A collection’s existence does not make every past life recoverable, and the website’s description is not a substitute for opening each record.

### The question underneath

What counts as evidence when nobody important thought your life worth filing?

The 1978 newsletter’s mission statement was inspected separately; most collection items were not read.

## Combahee: political theory required travel money, meals and relationships

### Place and period

Mid-to-late 1970s; recalled in 2003

Barbara Smith's oral history describes the Combahee River Collective and related Black feminist retreats as settings where political analysis, cultural exchange and ordinary logistics met. Participants pooled travel money and borrowed homes; serious discussion shared time with food and performances. Smith recalled Audre Lorde, Cheryl Clarke and Gloria Hull among those contributing cultural work. These recollections show ideas developing through relationships and material arrangements, not only through a finished manifesto.

Smith also acknowledged personal conflicts, including tensions around friendship, attraction and attachment, while declining to narrate private details. That boundary deserves respect: desire mattered within organizing, but it does not explain away the politics. Her account gives a useful alternative to either saintly unity or gossip. A group could produce enduring work while its members struggled with intimacy, disagreement and the pressure of depending deeply on one another.

### The question underneath

How can political intimacy support collective work without turning friendship into an obligation to agree?

### Evidence limit

This is Smith's retrospective account; she explicitly expresses uncertainty about the first retreat's year.

## Audre Lorde: desire as knowledge, pleasure as a political question

### Place and period

1978

In Uses of the Erotic, Audre Lorde argues that deep feeling and the capacity for joy can inform how people judge their work, relationships and political lives. Her erotic is wider than sexual activity: she connects embodied pleasure, creative effort and the experience of sharing with others. This argument challenges arrangements that measure work only through profit or treat emotional needs as irrelevant.

Lorde writes from her position as a Black lesbian feminist and links meaningful shared experience with the possibility of collective action. She also distinguishes sharing another person's feelings from using that person, making consent part of the argument. Read historically, this is a forceful intervention into how desire and power might connect, not proof of an innate feminine essence or a checklist that every lesbian must satisfy.

### The question underneath

What changes when pleasure becomes a question about meaningful work and mutuality, as well as sex?

### Evidence limit

Lorde's theoretical claims are attributed to her; this reproduction is not a critical scholarly edition.

Nigga, I had funded a committee that could recognize bad work immediately. It was proving expensive in ways I had not budgeted.

## Chicana lesbian thought: a coalition must remember who built it

### Place and period

1981 anthology; Moraga's 2015 retrospective, reprinted in 2016

Cherríe Moraga's Chicana lesbian writing places sexuality beside language, family and political belonging. She coedited This Bridge Called My Back with Gloria Anzaldúa in 1981, assembling different literary and artistic forms around women of color's lives. This was a coalition project, not a claim that every contributor occupied the same position. Moraga's own work moves between Spanish and English, poetry and prose, making form part of the encounter rather than treating theory as something detached from a life.

In a later preface excerpt, Moraga argues that political memory matters: movements lose something when each generation imagines itself the first to invent resistance. Her argument connects intimate and institutional conflicts with work, migration and place. Read together, these selected sources suggest a demanding question for coalition: whose lived knowledge becomes the foundation, and whose becomes an optional addition? That is our synthesis of the excerpts, not a summary of every essay in the anthology.

### The question underneath

Who gets treated as a source of political theory, and who is merely invited to supply an illustrative personal story?

### Evidence limit

This is a US Chicana contribution to a wider coalition, not a substitute for every Latina or Latin American lesbian history.

The reading list was under the buffet's short leg. Rae retrieved it, repaired the table and asked whether my keynote had any other structural applications.

Nigga, I gave the first ten minutes to somebody who had arrived knowing something.

## Pleasure and danger were not obliged to become enemy nations

### Place and period

Barnard sexuality conference, 1982

Barnard’s retrospective account describes the 1982 Scholar and Feminist conference as a flashpoint in arguments over sexuality. The planners wanted to address both sexual violence and women’s right to pleasure. A diary documenting preparation, writing and artwork became the focus of controversy; the college attempted to confiscate it and later paid for a reprint without its name. The institutional response belongs to the history of the argument, not just its publicity.

The retrospective criticizes a division that framed participants as either pro-sex or anti-violence. That opposition concealed the conference’s attempt to think about both. This does not mean all positions were compatible or that harms were imaginary. It gives our fiction a better problem than ‘the fun lesbians defeat the prudish ones’: how can people discuss coercion, erotic possibility and unequal power without pretending one concern automatically answers the others? The question remains a question rather than an official verdict on the entire feminist sex wars.

### The question underneath

Who gets lost when pleasure and protection are treated as mutually exclusive loyalties?

### Evidence limit

This account is one retrospective perspective on a larger, contested history.

The contractor sent an invoice for innovative joinery. For once, I paid without a speech.

## Punk, clubs, sex and politics occupy the same room

### Place and period

Rebel Dykes, London, 1980s–early 1990s

Bishopsgate Institute’s Rebel Dykes collection describes a network of lesbians and punk women in London whose lives connected art, music, club nights and political organizing. The archive names activity around Greenham Common, the South London Women’s Hospital occupation, anti-censorship, sex workers’ rights, opposition to Section 28 and HIV/AIDS activism. Its holdings include footage, images and later oral histories connected with Chain Reaction and the SM community.

The useful point is not that this network represents all British lesbians or that everyone agreed about sex. A locally specific scene can combine pleasure, practical mutual reliance and controversial politics. A club is not necessarily a holiday from history; it can be one of the places history is made. That interpretation also resists flattening the past into either respectable petitioners or a costume party. Here the details are drawn from the collection description, while the recordings themselves remain a further-reading route.

### The question underneath

What kinds of organizing become visible if the dance floor counts as a serious place?

### Evidence limit

A particular London network, not a universal account of lesbian sexual culture.

## Women were people with AIDS, organizers and caregivers

### Place and period

ACT UP and women’s AIDS activism, late 1980s–1990s

The ACT UP Oral History Project’s Women & AIDS page insists on several roles at once: women living with AIDS, movement leaders and caregivers. Its materials describe organizing over the CDC definition of AIDS, women’s access to services, prison conditions and peer support. The page also identifies work by Maxine Wolfe, Sarah Schulman, Catherine Gund and other participants. A lesbian history that mentions only care for gay men would miss the political agency and varied lives represented here.

The site is an activist archive, and its framing should be identified as such. For this guide, the inspected evidence is its descriptions of films, printed materials and campaigns; we did not watch every recording. Our interpretive connection is to coalition work: sharing a movement does not guarantee that everyone’s urgent needs appear in its public story. Counting people, funding services and changing institutional criteria are also political acts. This is historical context, not present-day medical advice.

### The question underneath

Who becomes a patient, a leader or only somebody else’s helper in the movement’s memory?

### Evidence limit

No claim that all women in this archive were lesbians; no simplistic origin story for acronym order.

## Wabanaki perspectives: a shared term does not erase a nation's own names

### Place and period

1990 terminology milestone; Wabanaki organizing from 2009

The Wabanaki Two-Spirit Alliance explains that Two-Spirit was introduced at the 1990 International Indigenous Lesbian and Gay Gathering in Winnipeg. A shared term could support reclamation without replacing the names, teachings or roles of individual nations. Its account connects identity with kinship, land, language and responsibilities; a translation concerned only with sexual attraction would miss part of what is being described.

The Alliance traces its own beginnings to a 2009 gathering responding to isolation and loss, while emphasizing cultural connection, celebration and life. It includes people who name themselves in several ways. Some Indigenous people identify as lesbian or queer without identifying as Two-Spirit; neither label authorizes an outsider to assign the other. For a lesbian history appendix, this is a necessary boundary as well as a connection: solidarity can support another community's self-definition without absorbing it into a familiar identity category.

### The question underneath

Can a coalition share resources without demanding that every participant translate themselves into its organizer's preferred categories?

### Evidence limit

Two-Spirit is not a universal Indigenous identity or a synonym for lesbian; this account reflects one regional alliance.

I said the manufacturer called it professional. Kit printed AIDEN on a blank card and handed me a pen.

The remaining space was for whatever I learned next. It was a humiliatingly large card.

## Visibility becomes an action, not a compliment

### Place and period

Lesbian Avengers, 1992–1993

The Lesbian Avenger Documentary Project dates the New York group’s beginnings to 1992 and names six experienced founders: Ana Simo, Sarah Schulman, Maxine Wolfe, Anne-christine d’Adesky, Marie Honan and Anne Maguire. Its account connects the first action to the fight over Queens’s multicultural Children of the Rainbow curriculum and to frustration with lesbian invisibility. Media and visually striking action were tools, not incidental decorations.

The project describes the 1993 Washington Dyke March as a major moment in the group’s expansion. Reading its own history shows both specificity and circulation: a local strategy could inspire other chapters without giving a single office ownership of every lesbian demand. Our editorial question is about who is seen and on whose terms. Visibility can mean appearing in somebody else’s photograph, or deciding what action puts a previously neglected issue in front of the public. Those are not interchangeable achievements.

### The question underneath

Are people merely visible, or do they control what the public is being asked to notice?

### Evidence limit

The account calls itself incomplete; chapter experiences should not be treated as identical.

## Gauteng: Nkateko and the placards that remain

### Place and period

1996–1998

GALA's guide records Nkateko, founded in Gauteng by Beverley Palesa Ditsie in 1996. It describes the constituency using period language for Black lesbian, bisexual and transgender gay women. The group participated in Johannesburg Pride in 1997 and dissolved in 1998. Collection AM 2661 contains organizational information and 22 handmade placards from that Pride.

This modest inventory changes what a historical story can notice. A short-lived organization can leave evidence of collective expression without becoming a lasting institution. The placards invite investigation of how participants presented themselves, although we read the catalog rather than the signs. Our interpretation remains limited: traces of agency and gathering cannot supply the group's complete internal history. Its disagreements, pleasures and reasons for ending remain questions to explore in the collection.

### The question underneath

Which movements disappear when longevity and famous leaders determine what counts as historically important?

### Evidence limit

Historical group terminology does not establish every participant's identity or explain the dissolution.

The foundry called about the deposit. I asked whether they could cast a cancellation instead.

## Kolkata: support, public argument and a magazine in one's own voice

### Place and period

1999–2004 founding and early publishing milestones

Sappho began in Kolkata in June 1999 as a self-support group for lesbians, bisexual women and transmasculine people. The organization's retrospective describes a wish to share ordinary dreams and difficulties as well as desire. Sappho for Equality followed in October 2003 as a platform connecting community support to rights and wider social participation. These are related developments with different dates, not interchangeable names for a single founding moment.

In January 2004, the group published the first Swakanthey, its bilingual magazine, and distributed it at Kolkata's book fair. Art, poetry, prose and articles offered a public creative voice beyond organizational announcements. This history holds a useful tension: people may need an intimate place to belong and also want to address audiences beyond it. The group's account includes debating and revising its own approach; it is not a tidy march from private silence to a finished public freedom.

### The question underneath

How can a group speak publicly without making public visibility a condition of receiving friendship and support?

### Evidence limit

This Kolkata account cannot represent all of India or South Asia; transmasculine participants must not be relabeled as lesbians.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

The first issue of our summit magazine had twelve photographs of me and a generous half-column reserved for everybody's voices.

Mercedes asked whether voices came in smaller sizes now. Velvet laid her performance photograph over my centerfold. Remy placed a drawing on top of my chairman's message.

Shawna found the one picture where I was actually helping. They kept that one.

My publishing career survived, substantially reduced in square footage.

### Read scope

Sappho for Equality — About Us. Organization's Sappho and Sappho for Equality histories, including June 1999 and October 2003 milestones.

### Source

https://www.sapphokolkata.in/about-us

## The Philippines: GALANG puts economic life inside sexual politics

### Place and period

2008 founding and the organization's subsequent program account

GALANG describes beginnings in conversations among lesbian friends and its registration in the Philippines in August 2008. Its founders wanted organizing to confront the relationship between sexuality and poverty. The organization identifies itself as lesbian-initiated and lesbian-run, working with lesbians, bisexual women and trans men in urban poor communities. Its account therefore places employment, services and material resources inside the discussion of sexual and gender freedom.

The program description joins community leadership training and participatory research with policy advocacy. It also lists Tatsulok Komiks, a lesbian comic-book series, among its educational materials. Creative storytelling belongs here alongside practical organizing, rather than appearing only after material needs have been solved. These sources describe an organization's purposes and methods, not an independent evaluation of its results. Their challenge to this appendix is concrete: an account of recognition remains incomplete if it never asks how people gain the resources to live and organize.

### The question underneath

What changes when a sexual-freedom agenda treats access to work and services as central rather than supplementary?

### Evidence limit

The organization does not stand for every Filipino community; an alliance among LBT people does not erase their different identities.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

The gold-plated Visibility Award cost more than the transport reimbursements. The volunteers noticed because the reimbursements had not happened.

I proposed a photograph with the award. Rosa proposed paying people.

Shawna turned the trophy upside down and read the return policy. The cashier asked why I was returning it. I said we had discovered a more practical form of recognition.

Nigga, a bank transfer had none of the trophy's sparkle and considerably more fans.

### Read scope

### Source

https://www.galangphilippines.org/about/

### Read scope

GALANG Philippines — What We Do. Full indexed program description: capacity building, advocacy, research and institutional development; comics themselves not read.

### Source

https://www.galangphilippines.org/about/what-we-do/

## Stone is not the final boss of masculinity

### Place and period

Contemporary terminology, with historical inheritances

Ro White’s Autostraddle discussion draws on interviews and earlier lesbian writing to describe variation in stone identities. Some people use the word for firm limits on receiving sexual touch; others describe more specific boundaries. The article cautions against assuming that every stone person has the same explanation, history or relationship to gender. Its contemporary testimony is useful precisely because it does not yield a single personality profile.

For this book, the distinction is between self-description and an outsider’s prediction. Clothes, confidence, race or a partner’s femininity do not tell another person what contact is wanted. Nor is changing someone’s boundary a romantic achievement. Those are ethical conclusions we bring to the fiction, rather than instructions for an intimate act. A reader can learn vocabulary without treating it as a license to interrogate a stranger. The term may help someone communicate; the actual person still supplies the meaning that matters in that relationship.

### The question underneath

Does a label help a person speak, or are you using it to stop listening?

### Evidence limit

This is non-graphic discussion of identity, desire and boundaries; terminology varies.

### Aiden has entered the archive / fiction

I had designed a masculinity leaderboard. At the top was a photograph of a very large boot.

Rae asked what the boot had consented to. I said the image was licensed.

'Different question,' Nia said.

Kit liked the boot. June hated the heel. Shawna asked why a chart about other people had my signature across it.

Nigga, I deleted the ranking. The boot remained handsome and entirely unavailable for comment.

### Read scope

Ro White — The Gay B C’s of Sex: S Is for Stone. Article text including first-person interview accounts inspected through indexed retrieval; no participant treated as representative of all stone people.

### Source

https://www.autostraddle.com/stone-butch-definition/

## Cultural reading notes

These are cultural reading notes, not a taxonomy of people. The dialogues are original fiction: each character has a partial perspective and no character speaks for an entire community. The fictional 1967 feud is not actual LGBTQ history. The notes below distinguish what was inspected from what was not.

### C1. Black lesbian gender and sexual culture: celebration and resistance

Wilson’s qualitative study describes gender and sexual roles in one African American lesbian community as sources of both expectations and resistance. That situated finding cautions against treating a character’s label as a universal rule about behavior, desire or power.

### Read scope

Abstract only; full article not inspected for this revision.

### Source

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19296308/

### C2. Brown Boi Project — About Us

The organization describes work among masculine-of-center women and queer and trans people of color across racial and gender justice. Its account helps frame masculinity as something people can enjoy, examine and change without assuming identical experiences or power.

### Read scope

Organizational self-description and participant testimony on the About Us page.

### Source

https://www.brownboiproject.org/about-us.html

### C3. The Combahee River Collective Statement

The collective connects race, gender, sexuality and class, and pairs solidarity with criticism of sexism. Its position informs the distinction between cooperation and erasure of internal conflict. It is a specific 1977 political statement; it is not evidence for the invented 1967 feud.

### Read scope

Selected sections of the primary statement, especially pages 1–4 of this reproduction.

### Source

https://lgbtqhistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/Combahee_River_Collective_Statement.pdf

### C4. Stone Butch Blues — selected author notes

These notes emphasize context, changing terminology, self-definition and collective connection. They provide a reason to let different generations use language differently, rather than force every fictional person into a single present-day vocabulary. The novel’s scenes and prose are not reproduced.

### Read scope

Selected author notes, printed pages 333–335 / PDF pages 350–352. No fresh full reading of the novel is claimed.

### Source

https://www.lesliefeinberg.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Stone-Butch-Blues-by-Leslie-Feinberg.pdf

### C5. What Is a Stud? The History of Black Lesbian Masculinity

The interviewees describe varied personal expressions of stud identity, including nonbinary experience, within Black queer culture. These accounts resist a checklist of clothes, sexual roles or personality traits. The fictional Rae speaks for herself.

### Read scope

Brief use of first-person interviews with Cortney Matthewis and $leazy EZ; no interview quotations reused.

### Source

https://www.them.us/story/what-is-a-stud-the-history-of-black-lesbian-masculinity

### C6. The Gender of Desire: Joan Nestle’s Last Interview — Our Dyke Histories

Nestle’s first-person account brings pleasure, class, race and risk into the same social world. It helps foreground femme desire and agency, rather than making a femme character a passive partner or a reward. No interview scene or erotic passage is adapted.

### Read scope

Selected written interview/transcript passages; audio not auditioned.

### Source

https://www.queergeographies.com/the-gender-of-desire-joan-nestles-last-interview/

### C7. Mabel Hampton Oral History Project — Reflections on Lesbian Fashion

The exhibit’s presentation of Hampton helps check against erasing Black butch lives or equating butchness with whiteness. Clothing and self-description belong to a particular life. June is an invented character, not a portrait of Hampton.

### Read scope

Curatorial descriptions inspected; recordings not auditioned and no new transcript made.

### Source

https://herstories.prattinfoschool.nyc/omeka/exhibits/show/reflections-on-lesbian-fashion/mabel-hampton-oral-history-pro

### C8. Sylvia Rivera’s 1973 speech — transcript in Document Set 3

Rivera’s speech challenges exclusion within a movement and asks who provides material support to vulnerable community members. It informs the coalition’s concern with paid work, resources and accountability. Rivera does not appear in the fiction, and no speech is assigned to a fictional character.

### Read scope

Speech transcript on PDF page 2. The packet’s Stonewall biographical claim is not relied upon.

### Source

https://teachrock.org/wp-content/uploads/Document-Set-3-Sylvia-Rivera.pdf

## Credits and source limits

Creative direction: Nolan. The Second Great Butch vs. Stud War / Coalition Edition: new ChatGPT-generated comic prose and production, retaining the researched game cards and selection mechanics. This is a separate user-directed alternate companion; previous editions and source novels remain intact. All fictional participants are adults; Lillian remains the reader.

Revision base: the Tellings Cut at Sodelin/Ten-Toes-Down commit 0e3fd666e7e1a0907e1e4dcd8ed3213cfee79a04. The earlier edition was grounded in sampled Niggatorial Tellings passages. The new summit cast, caucuses, romances and treaty are original companion fiction; they are not represented as recovered source canon. Editorial notes record the reading and rewriting scope.

The optional traits, tokens and signed-dice layer take inspiration from Fate. The Panorama’s catalogue coordinates, vetoes, snack amendment, incidents and appeals are original comic selection rules; this is not a substitute for the Fate rulebooks.

Fate reference pages consulted: https://fate-srd.com/fate-accelerated/how-do-stuff-outcomes-actions-and-approaches and https://fate-srd.com/fate-accelerated/aspects-fate-points . No Fate logos, illustrations or fonts are used.

This work is based on Fate Core System and Fate Accelerated Edition, products of Evil Hat Productions, LLC, developed, authored, and edited by Leonard Balsera, Brian Engard, Jeremy Keller, Ryan Macklin, Mike Olson, Clark Valentine, Amanda Valentine, Fred Hicks, and Rob Donoghue, and licensed for our use under the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/).

Game titles identify the corresponding games. No game code, ROMs, full manuals or third-party artwork are included. Availability and controls can vary by edition, region and platform. The sources support their stated claims; no purchase, installation or personal fit has been established by this book.

This edition includes frequent non-hateful reclaimed in-group language, strong profanity, fictional cocaine references and consensual non-graphic sexual innuendo. The fictional crew chorus intentionally repeats the reclaimed plural fifteen times on each fixed PDF page, separate from game facts. EPUB pagination is reflowable; its chorus appears at chapter boundaries. Fiction does not describe developers, real readers or entire identity groups.

The First Great Butch vs. Stud War of 1967, the Blue Comet Social Club, its veterans and the present summit are fictional. They are not claims about actual LGBTQ history. The book uses overlapping personal identities and individual disagreements rather than treating butches, studs, lesbians, drag performers and trans people as mutually exclusive populations.
